extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.
passages: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind.
Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data.

Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots.
“The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi.

“This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy.
Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’.

So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools.

Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies.
In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators.

In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain.

When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed.

“From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X.
“Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private.
Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior.

Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate.

It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it.

Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data.
Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44.
Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed.

RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline.

Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security.
Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept.
Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data.
For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be.
Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real.
“Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website.

And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains.

He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years.

In the tool, you describe what you want in a prompt, and AI does the rest. While the app is under creation, you’ll see options to add features you might have missed. You can make light edits once the app is complete, or you can completely scrap it and start again. There’s no charge to experiment and build an app. Custom Android apps make app development a much more personal and potentially user-friendly experience. It could be a fantastic option for replacing apps on your phone that you only use for a single thing – like a habit tracker, a calculator or converter, or a specific counter or timer. Perhaps the best part about this system is that an app you make doesn’t have to be commercially viable, and it doesn’t even have to be an app that anyone else needs. It just has to work for you . sources.title: Google wants to host your personal vibe-coded apps in the Play Store
passages: There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio.
This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system.

The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder.
Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products.
This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result.
Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family.
Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings.
It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries.
You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts.
Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon.
The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months.
You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations.
There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games.
Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.”
Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases.
Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games.
It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA.

extraction.body: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases. Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. For people who have embraced AI to build their own apps, the Play Store will soon offer a way to privately host and share those creations. Google rolled out Ask Play in 2025 as a small chatbot interface on Play Store listings. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA. You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.” Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. Anyone who has been tinkering with vibe-coded apps in AI Studio will soon have a direct pipe into the Play Store. This is not the same as publishing an app as a developer, but that could be the end result. There won’t be any tedious downloading of APK files or tinkering with a developer console—you’ll be able to send apps to the Play Store right from AI Studio. Adding a vibe coded app to the Play Store creates a “Personal Library” accessible from the app store client on your device. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system. Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google. Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months. extraction.body: Security researcher Dor Zvi and his team at the cybersecurity firm he cofounded, RedAccess, analyzed thousands of vibe-coded web applications created using the AI software development tools Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify and found more than 5,000 of them that had virtually no security or authentication of any kind. Many of these web apps allowed anyone who merely finds their web URL to access the apps and their data. Around 40 percent of the apps exposed sensitive data, Zvi says, including medical information, financial data, corporate presentations, and strategy documents, as well as detailed logs of customer conversations with chatbots. “The end result is that organizations are actually leaking private data through vibe-coding applications,” says Zvi. “This is one of the biggest events ever where people are exposing corporate or other sensitive information to anyone in the world.” Zvi says RedAccess’ scouring for vulnerable web apps was surprisingly easy. Lovable, Replit, Base44, and Netlify all allow users to host their web apps on those AI companies' own domains, rather than the users’. So the researchers used straightforward Google and Bing searches for those AI companies' domains combined with other search terms to identify thousands of apps that had been vibe coded with the companies' tools. Of the 5,000 AI-coded apps that Zvi says were left publicly accessible to anyone who simply typed their URLs into a browser, he found close to 2,000 that, upon closer inspection, seemed to reveal private data: Screenshots of web apps he shared with WIRED—several of which WIRED verified were still online and exposed—showed what appeared to be a hospital's work assignments with the personally identifiable information of doctors, a company's detailed ad purchasing information, what appeared to be another firm's go-to-market strategy presentation, a retailer's full logs of its chatbot's conversations with customers, including the customers' full names and contact information, a shipping firm's cargo records, and assorted sales and financial records from a variety of other companies. In some cases, Zvi says, he found that the exposed apps would have allowed him to gain administrative privileges over systems and even remove other administrators. In the case of Lovable, Zvi says he also found numerous examples of phishing sites that impersonated major corporations, including Bank of America, Costco, FedEx, Trader Joe’s, and McDonald’s, that appeared to have been created with the AI coding tool and hosted on Lovable's domain. When WIRED asked the four AI coding companies about RedAccess’ findings, Netlify didn’t respond, but the three other companies pushed back on the researchers’ claims and protested that they hadn't shared enough of their findings or provided enough time for them to respond. (RedAccess says it reached out to the companies on Monday.) But they didn't deny that the web apps RedAccess found were left exposed. “From the limited information they shared, [RedAccess's] core claim appears to be that some users have published apps on the open web that should’ve been private,” Replit's CEO Amjad Masad wrote in a response post on X. “Replit allows users to choose whether apps are public or private. Public apps being accessible on the internet is expected behavior. Privacy settings can be changed at any time with a single click.” A spokesperson for Lovable responded in a statement that “Lovable takes reports of exposed data and phishing sites seriously, and we're actively working to obtain what we need to investigate. It's also worth noting that Lovable gives builders the tools to build securely, but how an app is configured is ultimately the creator's responsibility.” Blake Brodie, the head of public relations for Base44's parent company, Wix, wrote in a statement that “Base44 provides users with robust tools to configure their own applications' security, including access controls and visibility settings.” She added that “disabling those controls is a deliberate, straightforward action, any user can do it. Where applications were publicly accessible, that reflects a user configuration choice, not a platform vulnerability.” Brodie also noted that “it is trivially easy to fabricate applications that appear to contain real user data. Without a single verified example provided to us, we have no way to assess the validity of these claims.” RedAccess, for its part, disputed that it hadn't provided examples to Base44. Zvi notes that for a few dozen exposed web apps, it went so far as to contact the app's apparent owner, which confirmed that data had been exposed. RedAccess also shared with WIRED anonymized communications in several cases that showed Base44 users thanking the researchers for alerting them to exposed web apps, which were then secured or taken offline. Verifying whether real data has been exposed on any particular unsecured AI-coded web app can be tricky, says Joel Margolis, a security researcher who, along with a colleague, recently discovered that an AI chat toy had exposed 50,000 conversations the toy had with children on a website with virtually no security. Data in a vibe-coded web app might be a placeholder, he says, or the app might be just a proof of concept. Wix’s Brodie argued that two examples that WIRED shared with Base44 did appear to be test sites or have AI-generated data. For the web apps WIRED reviewed, we couldn't confirm that the personal or corporate data was as sensitive—or real—as it appeared to be. Margolis nonetheless says that the problem of AI-built web apps exposing data is very real. “Somebody from a marketing team wants to create a website. And unless you ask them to do it securely, they're not going to go out of their way to do that.” Zvi points out that the 5,000 exposed apps Red Access found were only those hosted on the AI coding tools' own domains, and that likely thousands more are hosted on users' own purchased domains. He compares the ongoing deluge of data exposures that are resulting from companies' unsecured AI-coded web apps to the epidemic of exposed data created by the security settings of Amazon S3 storage buckets in earlier years. Companies from Verizon to World Wrestling Entertainment accidentally exposed reams of sensitive data due to misconfigurations in their instance of Amazon's cloud storage service. AI web-app coding tools are now creating a wave of data exposures, the result of a similar combination of user error and lack of safeguards, Zvi says. Yet more fundamental than any particular security failing on the part of the AI coding companies, he argues, is simply that these tools allow a new class of people within organizations to create applications—often with little security awareness and outside the usual software development processes that companies use to vet applications before they're released. “Anyone from your company at any moment can generate an app, and this is not going through any development cycle or any security check,” Zvi says. “People can just start using it in production without asking anyone.

extraction.body: Google plans to help turn those personal AI-generated apps into wide releases. Google has already added a few AI features to the Play Store, but a lot more are coming . The previously released Ask Play feature is expanding to offer more AI-powered discovery options in Google’s app store, and Google is also using AI to build a recommendation engine called Game Finder. It lets you ask questions about an app or game, either by typing it in manually or choosing from a list of suggested queries. Starting today, Ask Play is expanding into a more general way to search for apps and games. You ask the robot questions, and it generates recommendations that can include detailed comparison charts. Gemini will roll out a similar capability soon. Google’s other AI discovery announcement focuses on games. The new Game Finder feature leans on all the usage data Google’s app platform has hoovered up over the years, featuring insights into the way 1.2 billion people play games on Android. It builds a profile called Gamer DNA and matches you with players who have similar DNA. You can tune your DNA profile by rating the games you’ve played, which supposedly leads to more accurate recommendations. There will be game playlists to peruse, along with various contextual lists like relaxing, trending titles, and more specific lists based on mechanics you’ve seen in previous games. Game Finder also lets you add or remove tags to further adjust the games Google’s AI suggests. Google says you’ll eventually be able to prompt Game Finder with fairly specific game preferences, but it’s unclear how much customization will be available at launch. Game Finder and Gamer DNA are rolling out in the US today, with other markets following “soon.” Despite its slow progress in coding-focused AI models lately, Google is continuing to push this as a core feature of its products. This is available only to you by default, providing an easy way to install and manage the apps via Google’s system. Google says you can share these apps with “a small group” of friends and family. Google has not decided how many people count as a small group yet, but this type of distribution doesn’t require a developer account. If you want to share beyond that, Google plans to have an onboarding process to set you up with a developer profile to publish your vibe coded apps. If you do this, you’ll be subject to the same app review guidelines as developers who come into Google Play in the traditional way. Private apps are not reviewed by Google. Private vibe-coded apps in the Play Store will begin rolling out today in the US and select other markets. The private-to-public app migration option will be available in the coming months. extraction.body: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said on Wednesday that the Trump administration trusts Anthropic and the company is "back on the right side." A federal judge ruled in August that the Pentagon illegally punished Anthropic and struck down its blacklisting as a supply-chain risk. Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown has taken a larger role in repairing the AI firm's relationship with the White House following tensions over military use of its models. Anthropic remains designated as a supply chain risk by the U.S. Department of Defense and the defense industry, despite Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick saying the AI company is "back on the right side." Emil Michael, under secretary of defense for research and engineering, said on Thursday that Anthropic is still considered a "supply chain risk" by the Pentagon. Michael wrote in a post on X, "Anthropic is still a designated Supply Chain Risk at @DeptofWar and for the Defense Industrial Base." See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox His remarks came a day after Lutnick's comments signaled a potential thaw in relations between the AI company and the Trump administration. On Wednesday, Lutnick told Axios on the sidelines of the G20 Innovation Summit, "We trust Anthropic." When asked whether he trusts Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Lutnick said, "They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes." Lutnick's comments came as Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown takes a larger role in managing the company's relationship with the White House, including a headlining appearance at this week's G20 Innovation Ministerial. In August, a federal judge also struck down the Pentagon's blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain risk. The judge ruled in favor of Anthropic on August 27, determining that the Pentagon illegally punished the AI company for criticizing the government and that its decision was "baseless," according to Axios. However, Anthropic is still fighting a separate Pentagon designation under a different statute in the D.C. Circuit. The Trump administration is not entirely aligned on Anthropic following months of fighting over how the military can use its models. Earlier this year, tensions between the Trump administration and Anthropic escalated amid personality differences, culminating in sweeping export controls on the company's most advanced models. Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown played an instrumental role in repairing the relationship, holding multiple conversations with Howard Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. passages: Anthropic has asked a federal appeals court in Washington, US, to rehear its appeal in the case concerning the Pentagon’s decision to designate the company as a supply chain risk.

sources.title: Apple releases HomeView smart home hub with screen as showcase for Siri AI - CNBC
passages: Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it.
Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday.
Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

13 in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand.

Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself.

Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

Apple says users can view as many as nine live camera feeds at once and control connected devices through the screen or Siri.

extraction.body: Apple has opened preorders for HomeView, a $299 smart display intended to sit at the center of a connected household. The 7-inch device combines touch controls for lights, locks and cameras with FaceTime, speakers, personalized household screens and Siri AI. It goes on sale Nov. 13 in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, India and New Zealand. The launch gives Apple a direct answer to screen-equipped home hubs from Amazon and Google, a category where Apple has largely relied on iPads, HomePods and third-party accessories. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people, while its most sensitive personalized functions require an eligible, nearby and recently unlocked iPhone or iPad. According to Apple’s HomeView announcement , the device has a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and an A18 chip. It is available as a tabletop model or a wall-mounted model, both listed at $299 in the United States. The wall version requires a separate Schneider Home mount. Apple lists USB-C and AC-wired mounts at $59.95 and $79.95, respectively, while a Power over Ethernet mount priced at $129.95 is not expected until early 2027. Apple says HomeView can recognize up to six people and show personalized calendars, reminders, photo collections and home controls. CNBC’s launch coverage also describes the device as a showcase for the company’s Siri AI effort and household-profile system. Recognition does not by itself open a person’s private material. Apple says personal content requires that user’s paired iPhone or iPad to be nearby and recently unlocked. Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. Apple describes HomeView as a shared device for household tasks while keeping personal content tied to a user’s paired device. Apple also says camera and microphone information is processed in protected hardware runtimes unavailable to HomeView software, apps, users or Apple itself. The company presents those protections as part of its privacy approach. HomeView is a touch-and-voice controller for compatible Apple Home and Matter accessories. Apple says users can view as many as nine live camera feeds at once and control connected devices through the screen or Siri. Apple is also using HomeView to promote its Apple Home Collection, a group of accessories developed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. CNET’s launch coverage cites Ben Wood, chief analyst at CCS Insight, saying Apple has made setup for the new home products simpler than alternatives that require separate apps and QR-code scanning. Apple’s announcement says HomeView works with Apple TV and compatible third-party audio and video apps. The release does not provide a service-by-service list or clearly state which video apps run directly on HomeView and which require an iPhone, iPad or another Apple device. WIRED’s hands-on report says HomeView has no App Store and that YouTube, Netflix and Disney+ were not available as native apps at the time of its briefing. AppleInsider reported that video playback may depend on AirPlay from an iPhone or iPad or on CarPlay-related functionality. The available reporting does not resolve which services Apple considers compatible video apps. Preorders began Oct. 13 in the first group of markets. Apple says Singapore preorders begin Oct. 15. South Africa is scheduled to receive HomeView on Nov. 13 through authorized resellers. Apple says HomeView will not be sold in the European Union at launch because Siri AI is unavailable in iOS there. Siri AI is labeled beta in HomeView software version 27.2, and Apple says its personal-context capabilities require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. HomeView becomes available Nov. 13 in Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the United Kingdom and the United States.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad.

"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.

The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it.
Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday.
Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence.
People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.

Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories.
But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage.
It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.

Personal-context Siri requests also require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad.

extraction.body: Following the incident on a Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv, U.S. media are reporting on explosive details about the suspected attacker. (File photo) Following the violent incident in the cockpit of a Flydubai aircraft, several details remain unclear. U.S. media are now reporting explosive new information about the alleged attacker. According to U.S. media reports, the co-pilot who is alleged to have injured the pilot of the Flydubai flight to Tel Aviv had previously been fired from his former job at an airline in Oman due to security concerns. ABC News reports, citing high-ranking intelligence and law enforcement officials, that the man had been suspended by Oman Air after being deemed a security risk. According to information from the U.S. broadcaster, extremist material was found in the possession of the suspected attacker from Oman while he was employed by the airline as a co-pilot trainee in 2024. However, he was reportedly allowed to continue working there in an administrative role. The U.S. network CNN has received similar information. The *Wall Street Journal* reports, citing people familiar with the matter, that the man from Oman had previously been placed on a no-fly list. The reason for this was concern that he held radical ideological views. According to ABC News, investigators are currently trying to determine how he was subsequently allowed to fly for Flydubai. The arrested co-pilot, who has since been taken to the Emirates, is reportedly cooperating with investigators. He indicated that he had intended to crash the Flydubai plane in Israel, the network reports, citing sources familiar with the investigation. The Emirates flight was en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Wednesday when the co-pilot allegedly attacked his colleague. According to his own account, the pilot managed to open the cockpit door despite suffering serious injuries. Several passengers entered the cockpit and were able to subdue the attacker. Emirati authorities have launched an investigation; the motive and intentions of the suspected attacker remain unclear. The Israeli government is already treating the incident as a jihadist terrorist attack—and a high-ranking government official from the United Arab Emirates also recently referred to the violent act as terrorism. The U.S. news network CNN reports on a LinkedIn profile that is said to have existed under the alleged attacker’s name and has since been deleted. Two posts are said to have been published on this profile hours after the attack. It is unclear who posted them or whether they had been planned in advance. According to CNN, one of the posts contained a video that ends, among other things, with a photo of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri.

Multiple sources familiar with the investigation identified the suspected attacker as 29-year-old Hamam Al Hammami. The officials told ABC News that Al Hammami, while working as a co-pilot trainee for Oman Air in 2024, was found to be in possession of extremist materials. The suspect was allowed to continue working for the airline in an administrative role, the sources said. United Arab Emirates Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Saturday said the aircraft's co-pilot had attempted to carry out a terrorist act and that he began executing his plan during the flight by assaulting the pilot inside the cockpit using a crash axe and attempted to seize control of the aircraft's controls, according to WAM state news agency. This is the first confirmation by UAE authorities that the co-pilot had attacked the captain and identified the weapon used as a crash axe. Previous UAE statements had described the incident as a security incident and said an investigation was underway to determine whether it involved terrorist activity or prior planning. The attorney general stressed that investigations are still ongoing to establish all the circumstances and motives surrounding the incident, as well as any related links. He added that technical examinations and the analysis of physical and digital evidence are also being completed, with the final findings to be announced once the necessary procedures have been concluded. Officials investigating the incident are still trying to determine how the suspected attacker was subsequently permitted to fly for FlyDubai and how he ended up as the first officer in the cockpit of a plane headed for Israel, the sources said. Al Hammami -- who was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates -- is said to be "cooperating" with authorities investigating the incident and has indicated that his intent was to crash the aircraft in Israel, according to sources briefed on the investigation. "We recognise that there are many questions at this stage; however, the circumstances surrounding the incident are still under investigation," FlyDubai said in a statement obtained by ABC News on Saturday. "We are therefore not in a position to comment further beyond our published statements. We remain fully committed to supporting the ongoing investigation and are in close coordination with the relevant government authorities and regulators." Representatives for Oman Air and the Omani Embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News. FlyDubai issued a statement earlier Friday, attributed to its chief executive officer, saying that, at the request of the authorities, FlyDubai had "temporarily suspended operations to Tel Aviv until further notice," and saying "a full official investigation, led by the relevant authorities and fully supported by flydubai, is underway." A disaster was averted when the flight's captain, Smit Machchhar, fought back and a number of passengers subdued and restrained the attacker, who had sent the plane into a rapid dive . One of the passengers, Israeli plumber Yaniv Hayoun, said he pulled back on the controls to steady the plane until a third pilot, who was traveling in the passenger cabin, took over. The flight eventually landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. One of the passengers who ran to the front of the plane, Dr. Shota Musaev, told ABC News in an interview this week that the attacker -- who was bloodied and restrained on the floor outside the cockpit -- told him he was from Oman. Musaev said that at one point the suspect asked Musaev to kill him. "He said, 'Kill me please, kill me please,'" Musaev said. Israeli officials are expected to be on the ground and involved in the questioning of Al Hammami, sources said. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said that the suspected attacker, who he didn't name, had undergone "Islamist radicalization." The anticipated launch forms part of Apple's efforts to expand its presence in the connected home market, where it has competed for several years against Amazon and Google without establishing a dominant position. The new products are expected to provide centralised control over connected household devices, including video doorbells, thermostats and smart locks. Analysts have also suggested that Apple could introduce updated versions of its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV. The announcements come as the company seeks additional opportunities for hardware growth while facing increased competition in artificial intelligence and regulatory pressure on its services business. The centrepiece of the expected product announcements is a smart home control device designed for installation on a wall or placement on a tabletop. The device is expected to provide an interface for managing connected household equipment while incorporating Apple's enhanced Siri assistant. Its capabilities could allow users to interact with multiple smart home products through a single system, potentially simplifying everyday tasks such as adjusting heating, monitoring entrances and controlling electronic locks. Apple has been developing its connected home ecosystem for approximately a decade. The company introduced its Home application in 2016, followed by the HomePod smart speaker in 2018. However, its products have faced established competition from Amazon's Echo speakers and Google's Home devices. One of the main challenges has been ensuring compatibility with smart home products manufactured by third-party companies. A centralised interface may improve accessibility, but its effectiveness will depend on how easily users can connect and manage devices from different manufacturers. Apple's upgraded Siri virtual assistant is expected to be a significant feature of the new smart home products. The company improved Siri's capabilities during the summer with assistance from Google, seeking to address limitations in the assistant's ability to respond to questions and carry out more complex requests. Greater artificial intelligence functionality could make voice-controlled home management more useful, particularly when coordinating several connected devices. However, analysts have questioned whether improvements in Siri alone will be sufficient to encourage broader adoption of Apple's smart home products. Bob O'Donnell, chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, said that setting up connected home systems remains too complicated for many consumers. "Advances in AI should finally make a difference, but Apple still needs to show whether it can simplify connectivity and work with devices across the wider smart home market rather than restricting users to its own ecosystem," O'Donnell said. His comments highlighted the importance of interoperability alongside improvements in artificial intelligence. For Apple, making connected home technology easier to install and operate could be as important as introducing new hardware or expanding Siri's capabilities. Apple's planned product introductions come amid intensifying competition in the smart home and artificial intelligence markets. Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) has invested heavily in connected home technology through its Echo smart speakers and Ring video doorbells. The company also introduced premium tablets last week, expanding its range of consumer hardware products. Alphabet's Google (NASDAQ:GOOGL) remains another major competitor through its Google Home devices and associated smart home services. Meanwhile, newer artificial intelligence companies, including OpenAI, are exploring opportunities to develop consumer hardware. However, the company's ability to compete will depend partly on the compatibility, usability and functionality of its new products. The anticipated smart home expansion comes as investors pay closer attention to Apple's hardware sales as a potential source of future growth. The company's services business has faced regulatory scrutiny, increasing the importance of identifying additional revenue opportunities across its product portfolio. Smart home devices could provide another category through which Apple expands customer relationships and encourages the use of its existing products and services. However, the company has yet to achieve the same level of success in connected home technology as it has in smartphones, tablets and other consumer electronics. The expected announcements will therefore provide an indication of how Apple intends to strengthen its position in the market. passages: The HomeView smart-home hub, which took center stage at an event in New York, is an important test of Apple's AI strategy as it tries to close the gap with rivals Amazon and Alphabet's Google, while reinforcing its reputation for user privacy.
HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip.
To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself.
Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts.
HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen.
Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work.

"That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview.
Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user.

While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user.

extraction.body: NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Apple on Tuesday unveiled a smart-home hub that taps iPhone user data to make Siri more personal, but promised privacy safeguards designed to keep that information out of the company's hands. The HomeView smart-home hub, which took center stage at an event in New York, is an important test of Apple's AI strategy as it tries to close the gap with rivals Amazon and Alphabet's Google, while reinforcing its reputation for user privacy. In a series of demonstrations, Apple showed Siri AI recognizing a user's face and performing personalized tasks such as fetching recipes from text messages, finding a nearby farmer's market for missing ingredients and then updating shopping lists. When a different member of the household steps in, the HomeView recognizes that user's face and switches to their personal data, for example fetching information from text messages about when a friend's early morning flight lands and how long it will take them to arrive, then teeing up a coffee maker a few minutes ahead of time. The new device and Siri AI lean on the iPhone to make those personalized features happen, reflecting new CEO John Ternus' vision of Apple's best-selling product as an "intelligent personal hub" laid out at Apple's iPhone launch event last month. Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user. HomeView draws on a personal search index stored on the user's iPhone to personalize responses. "That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview. HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip. To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself. Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts. "One of the things we talked about is not building a marketing profile," Drance said. "Our intent is to provide users a helpful experience that adheres to simplicity, being personal, being intelligent, and continuing our commitment to privacy." A key difference between Siri AI and rival systems is that it does not end each interaction with a follow-up question designed to elicit more information from the user, a practice that Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, said was a deliberate choice on Apple's part. "For us, it's really about creating these really great products for consumers, which is why we're not in this game of getting you to engage and continue the conversation in many, many, many turns," Rincon said. HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen. Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work. While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user. "There is a logic built in to kind of manage that experience," Drance said. "There was thought put into the nature of that communal computer sharing of the voice and the face recognition."

The new device and Siri AI lean on the iPhone to make those personalized features happen, reflecting new CEO John Ternus' vision of Apple's best-selling product as an "intelligent personal hub" laid out at Apple's iPhone launch event last month.
Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user. HomeView draws on a personal search index stored on the user's iPhone to personalize responses.

"That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview.

HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip. To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself. Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts.

"One of the things we talked about is not building a marketing profile," Drance said. "Our intent is to provide users a helpful experience that adheres to simplicity, being personal, being intelligent, and continuing our commitment to privacy."

A key difference between Siri AI and rival systems is that it does not end each interaction with a follow-up question designed to elicit more information from the user, a practice that Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, said was a deliberate choice on Apple's part.

"For us, it's really about creating these really great products for consumers, which is why we're not in this game of getting you to engage and continue the conversation in many, many, many turns," Rincon said.

HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen. Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work.

While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user.
"There is a logic built in to kind of manage that experience," Drance said. "There was thought put into the nature of that communal computer sharing of the voice and the face recognition."

NEW YORK -- Apple on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market.

Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet’s Google Home speakers and Amazon’s Echo line.
It will feature a 7-inch screen and face recognition, will help users control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success.
Other bells and whistles Apple’s HomeView launch was accompanied by updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices.
Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers.

Apple stock has gained 25 per cent so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21 per cent for the same period. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; Additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by David Gaffen and Christian Plumb)

Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com, which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week launched premium tablets, as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own.
It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple.

extraction.body: NEW YORK -- Apple on Tuesday launched a raft of smart products, including an iPad-like device dubbed the HomeView, in a bet that its AI-upgraded Siri virtual assistant can help it carve out a bigger share of the highly competitive connected home market. The HomeView device, which starts at US$299 and starts shipping next month, is Apple’s latest entry into a highly competitive market for home connected devices. It will feature a 7-inch screen and face recognition, will help users control doorbells, thermostats and smart locks in a market where Apple has tinkered for a decade without major success. Apple is launching these products as it tries to fend off competition from rivals, including traditional competitors like Amazon.com, which has invested heavily in its Echo speakers and Ring doorbells and last week launched premium tablets, as well as newer AI upstarts like OpenAI that have hardware ambitions of their own. “Apple needs to demonstrate that its AI capabilities can deliver meaningful benefits beyond basic voice commands, simplifying everyday tasks and bringing greater intelligence to the home,” said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore. “The opportunity is considerable, given its vast installed base, but reliability, trust and ease of use will ultimately determine whether consumers embrace these features,” he added. “AI alone will not be enough to convince households to invest in more devices.” Investors are looking more closely at Apple’s hardware sales for growth as the company’s services revenue has come under regulatory pressure. Apple this summer upgraded Siri’s capabilities with assistance from Google but analysts said it is unclear whether its AI assistant is competitive enough to lure consumers to a crowded connected home device space. The launches also coincide with growing worries that connected devices, including refrigerators and smart TVs, could be vulnerable to hackers. Other bells and whistles Apple’s HomeView launch was accompanied by updates to its HomePod smart speaker and Apple TV devices. It also introduced a range of accessories, including doorbells, cameras and thermostats, made by LG and Schneider Electric and designed with help from Apple. “It is interesting to see Apple partnering with LG and Schneider, as it typically likes to have full control of the hardware it sells,” said Ben Wood, co-founder of CCS Insight. ”However, looking closely, it appears like there has been very deep collaboration between Apple and these partners to ensure the design, engineering and experience closely match what users would expect from Apple.” During a video demonstrating the device, Apple showed the HomeView, which is meant to hang on walls or perch on tabletops, and its Siri virtual assistant juggling voice requests from multiple members of a family at the same time. The HomeView device will not be sold in the European Union, because Siri AI remains unavailable there due to EU regulations, Apple said. Apple first released its Home app to control smart gadgets in 2016, with HomePod smart speakers following in 2018, but those offerings are competing with Alphabet’s Google Home speakers and Amazon’s Echo line. Analysts said two major hurdles for Apple were making its devices work with a variety of third-party gadgets and the limited ability of Siri to give useful answers. “Most smart speakers and hubs in homes today are low-cost devices that can’t run AI at the edge, so they are ripe for replacement,” said Mohit Agrawal, Research Director at Counterpoint. “Amazon and Google have only just begun refreshing their hardware for Alexa+ and Gemini, so the upgrade cycle is wide open, and Apple wants to win it.” Apple $299 price for HomeView is above Amazon’s Echo Show 8 at $199.99 and Google’s Nest Hub at $99.99, as it seeks a bigger role in connected homes. The new Apple TV 4K enters the market at $299, more than double the price of its predecessor and in line with Nvidia’s Shield TV Pro, while rival offerings from Amazon, Google and Roku cost $200 or less. Shares were up 1.6 per cent in early Tuesday trading. Apple stock has gained 25 per cent so far this year, outperforming the large-cap Nasdaq 100, which is up 21 per cent for the same period. (Reporting by Stephen Nellis in San Francisco; Additional reporting by Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by David Gaffen and Christian Plumb)

extraction.body: NEW YORK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Apple on Tuesday unveiled a smart-home hub that taps iPhone user data to make Siri more personal, but promised privacy safeguards designed to keep that information out of the company's hands. The HomeView smart-home hub, which took center stage at an event in New York, is an important test of Apple's AI strategy as it tries to close the gap with rivals Amazon and Alphabet's Google, while reinforcing its reputation for user privacy. In a series of demonstrations, Apple showed Siri AI recognizing a user's face and performing personalized tasks such as fetching recipes from text messages, finding a nearby farmer's market for missing ingredients and then updating shopping lists. When a different member of the household steps in, the HomeView recognizes that user's face and switches to their personal data, for example fetching information from text messages about when a friend's early morning flight lands and how long it will take them to arrive, then teeing up a coffee maker a few minutes ahead of time. The new device and Siri AI lean on the iPhone to make those personalized features happen, reflecting new CEO John Ternus' vision of Apple's best-selling product as an "intelligent personal hub" laid out at Apple's iPhone launch event last month. Siri AI's usefulness hinges on how much it knows about a user. HomeView draws on a personal search index stored on the user's iPhone to personalize responses. "That will give you what's more relevant, what's more timely, what's important to you, because it's coming from your iPhone," Kaiann Drance, Apple's vice president of product marketing for home products, said in an interview. HomeView has its own operating system and runs on Apple's A18 chip, designed to process encrypted user data in a walled-off part of the chip. To access private data, a user's iPhone has to be connected to the same home network as HomeView, and no private data is stored on the HomeView device itself. Apple said none of the data is used for marketing, including first-party advertising efforts. "One of the things we talked about is not building a marketing profile," Drance said. "Our intent is to provide users a helpful experience that adheres to simplicity, being personal, being intelligent, and continuing our commitment to privacy." A key difference between Siri AI and rival systems is that it does not end each interaction with a follow-up question designed to elicit more information from the user, a practice that Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, said was a deliberate choice on Apple's part. "For us, it's really about creating these really great products for consumers, which is why we're not in this game of getting you to engage and continue the conversation in many, many, many turns," Rincon said. HomeView also required Apple to figure out how to make Siri personal on a device shared by multiple people in communal spaces such as a kitchen. Apple demonstrated HomeView juggling requests from family members during the morning rush to school and work. While the device can recognize up to six voices and faces to show private data, Apple said it will make decisions on which user to prioritize based on who last touched the device and other factors, and that some features such as weather and thermostat controls will be available to any user. "There is a logic built in to kind of manage that experience," Drance said. "There was thought put into the nature of that communal computer sharing of the voice and the face recognition."

extraction.body: Strive, Inc. (Nasdaq: ASST), the bitcoin-focused structured finance company, plans to raise $500 million through a new perpetual preferred stock carrying a fixed 15% annual dividend, with bitcoin purchases listed as a primary use of the proceeds. The company disclosed the plan in a press release on Oct. 13. Subject to market conditions, the offering would sell 5 million shares of 15.00% Series A Perpetual SATS Preferred Stock at a stated amount of $100 per share. At 15%, the new security pays more than Strive’s existing variable-rate SATA preferred, currently set at 13%, and it ranks junior to SATA in the capital structure. Dividends accumulate at 15% per year on the $100 stated amount and are payable only when declared by Strive’s board, with regular payment dates beginning Nov. 9, 2026; the first scheduled payment would include dividends accrued from the closing date. Strive plans to set aside a reserve equal to 18 months of payments, $22.50 per share (about $112.5 million across the 5 million shares), funded with cash on hand and securities. Proceeds are earmarked for general corporate purposes, including bitcoin and bitcoin-related products, working capital, income-generating assets, capital expenditures, repurchases of common stock or SATA, and potential acquisitions. Barclays and Cantor are joint book-running managers, with Clear Street as lead manager, under an effective SEC shelf registration. Strive describes bitcoin as its “hurdle rate” for deploying capital, a benchmark any new commitment must be expected to clear. Paying a fixed 15% means the company is betting it can earn more than that cost by holding bitcoin, which traded near $83,400 early on Oct. 14, and by growing its income-generating assets. The 15% coupon is the price of subordination. SATS holders sit junior to SATA, so they receive a higher, fixed dividend for taking more risk. Unlike the convertible-debt financing favored by the largest bitcoin treasury, Strategy, which added 250 bitcoin in its latest weekly buy , preferred equity carries a visible cash dividend but no maturity or forced-conversion overhang. A fixed 15% cumulative dividend is a heavy, ongoing cash obligation of roughly $75 million a year if fully declared. The liquidation preference starts at $100 per share but adjusts daily in part to track SATS’s own market price, which can expose holders to downside beyond the stated amount. Strive may redeem the shares only if the outstanding count falls below 25% of those originally issued or on tax events, and holders gain a repurchase right only on a “fundamental change.” The offering is not yet priced and remains subject to market conditions, so the final terms and closing date are unresolved. The next observable steps are the pricing and completion of the deal, the first dividend date on Nov. 9, and whether Strive deploys the proceeds into bitcoin near current levels. Strive’s last disclosed treasury move was buying 1,355 bitcoin in late September , lifting its holdings to 26,355 BTC.

The company is aiming to sell 5 million shares at $100 per share, for a capital raise of $500 million, with proceeds to be used to purchase additional bitcoin BTC $83,212.45 , acquire income-producing assets, or buy back stock.

At closing of the offering, the company intends to establish a dividend reserve equal to the first 18 months of dividend payments on SATS.
The new share class will sit junior to Strive’s current perpetual preferred, SATA, which has a variable rate (currently 13%).
Like SATA, SATS will pay dividends on a daily basis.

Dividends accumulate at 15% per year on the $100 stated amount and are payable only when declared by Strive’s board, with regular payment dates beginning Nov.
9, 2026; the first scheduled payment would include dividends accrued from the closing date.
Strive plans to set aside a reserve equal to 18 months of payments, $22.50 per share (about $112.5 million across the 5 million shares), funded with cash on hand and securities.

SATS holders sit junior to SATA, so they receive a higher, fixed dividend for taking more risk.

The Strategy executive told Bloomberg Television he believes the bull market is just beginning and expects Bitcoin to move back above $100,000.
At the time of the report, BTC was trading at $83,761.77. Saylor said it had bounced from a low slightly below $60,000 and was moving into what he sees as more favorable conditions.
“I think we hit the bottom around slightly below $60,000. I think we bounced off it. Now we're moving up into the eighties. I think we'll continue to march forward from here,” Saylor said.

His view offers a sharp contrast with the pressures he said had weighed on prices in recent months. Saylor cited restrictive trade, foreign, currency and monetary policies as headwinds, while pointing to a more favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and growth in the digital asset market as potential support.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

“I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction.

Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares.

He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.

Saylor said Bitcoin was trading 25% above its two-hundred-week moving average after briefly dipping below it. He also described the development of digital credit networks and the arrival of banking credit as favorable for the asset.
“We've got the formation of and the strengthening of digital credit networks and, of course, banking credit coming online, and all these things are very auspicious for the asset,” he said.

The forecast matters to investors because it links Saylor’s optimism to a mix of market structure and policy conditions, rather than price momentum alone. But the figures remain his outlook, not a guarantee of future performance.

“I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000,” Saylor said. He added that Strategy’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.” He described the last twelve months as a contraction.

Strategy’s own trading policy also featured in the interview. Saylor said buying and selling Bitcoin is part of the company’s regular financial activity, alongside transactions involving dollars, equity, credit, STRC and its own shares.

He argued that the company needs flexibility to move among those assets and sources of capital. Saylor said that refusing to sell equity, capital or credit could degrade the company’s value, and described the ability to trade different asset pairs in either direction as a major unlock for investors.
Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total holdings to 848,250 BTC. The purchase was the company’s smallest Bitcoin buy in 2026.

For the week ended Oct. 9, Strategy sold 125,183 MSTR shares for $21 million and used the proceeds, along with $500 million from its USD Cash reserves, to fund its Bitcoin purchase. The company also repurchased 1.9 million STRC shares for $192.4 million.

Investor sentiment on Stocktwits was weak: retail sentiment around MSTR fell from “bearish” to “extremely bearish” over 24 hours amid low message volumes, while sentiment around BTC was “bearish,” also with low message volumes.
