sources.title: Saylor sees Bitcoin above $100,000, says investors will seek (scarce) assets that robots can’t make - investingLive
passages: Strategy co-founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin is entering a new bull market and should climb back above $100,000, arguing that artificial intelligence will push investors towards assets whose supply cannot be expanded.
These are Strategy’s income-paying securities, such as STRC, backed by the company’s Bitcoin holdings.
Saylor says they pay 10% to 12% a year, treated as a return of capital, which generally defers tax rather than removing it.
The company may sell Bitcoin or other assets to fund these payments, which is why it now says it must be free to sell as well as buy.
He declined to give a timeframe for his $100,000 target, saying he plans in centuries, not months.
Strategy’s longer-term forecast is for Bitcoin to grow 20% to 30% a year over the next two decades.

Friday’s upcoming MSCI decision on whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices is the nearest catalyst, since an exclusion could trigger passive selling of the shares even if Saylor plays down its importance.
On the positive side, regulatory guidance from US agencies has eased a key overhang.

Saylor argued that AI will reduce the value of companies built on large human workforces or on chasing the next breakthrough product, while increasing demand for scarce capital such as Palm Beach real estate, gold and Bitcoin.
In his words, investors will look for things robots cannot make more of.
By his own description, Bitcoin is also a volatile asset, with volatility of around 40, while Strategy’s shares run at roughly 80.
Saylor also defended Strategy’s sale of a small amount of Bitcoin in June, when prices were around $73,000, a move that unsettled the market.
Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy and listed under the ticker MSTR, started as an enterprise software company.
Since August 2020 it has focused on buying and holding Bitcoin, funded largely by issuing shares, debt and preferred-style securities.
It is now the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, with holdings Saylor puts at more than $70 billion.
If AI makes labour and software abundant, assets with fixed supply could gain relative appeal.

Bloomberg’s interviewers also challenged it, noting that AI is absorbing much of the market’s capital and that the scarcity rotation has yet to show clearly in Bitcoin, which remains about 30% below last year’s record high.
Fed's Williams sees no 2027 rate hike, diverging from trader bets as Bitcoin slips from $84k.
Saylor called the proposal a bad precedent, argued Strategy is an operating company like banks and insurers, and said the decision was not that important to the firm.
It would also set a precedent for the growing number of similar companies.
Saylor is talking his book, but his core pitch, that AI makes scarcity more valuable, is an argument worth weighing on its merits.

facts.text: "I think that it should definitely move back into the six figures, back beyond $100,000.
And our long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20 to 30% a year over the next twenty years.
So, clearly, the last twelve months have been a contraction," Saylor said.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Strategy's (MSTR) Michael Saylor believes the Bitcoin (BTC) bull market is just beginning, with the digital currency gaining market tailwinds after a tough few months.

When asked about Strategy's Bitcoin policy, Saylor said that as a finance company, buying and selling BTC was part of the regular process, just like buying or selling dollars, equity, credit, STRC, and its own shares.
The billionaire entrepreneur noted that, compared with the two-hundred-week moving average, Bitcoin prices dipped slightly below it, but added that BTC is now trading 25% above the average.
He said bitcoin is now moving into tailwinds, including a favorable regulatory environment, faster bank adoption, tokenized securities and a growing digital asset market.
Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total to 848,250 BTC.

In an interview with Bloomberg Television, Saylor said BTC prices would return to six figures and cross $100,000, adding that the company’s “long-term forecast is Bitcoin grows 20%-30% a year over the next twenty years.”What’s Driving Saylor’s Bullish Bitcoin Forecast?The billionaire entrepreneur noted that, compared with the two-hundred-week moving average, Bitcoin prices dipped slightly below it, but added that BTC is now trading 25% above the average.
Strategy’s (MSTR) Michael Saylor believes the Bitcoin (BTC) bull market is just beginning, with the digital currency gaining market tailwinds after a tough few months.

Strategy’s Stance On Bitcoin When asked about Strategy’s Bitcoin policy, Saylor said that as a finance company, buying and selling BTC was part of the regular process, just like buying or selling dollars, equity, credit, STRC, and its own shares.

And what we established this summer is the ability for the company to buy and sell the credit, buy and sell the equity, and buy and sell the Bitcoin, and that was a big unlock for all of our investors and every asset class.”Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total to 848,250 BTC.

Strategy co-founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin is entering a new bull market and should climb back above $100,000, arguing that artificial intelligence will push investors towards assets whose supply cannot be expanded.
These are Strategy’s income-paying securities, such as STRC, backed by the company’s Bitcoin holdings.
Saylor says they pay 10% to 12% a year, treated as a return of capital, which generally defers tax rather than removing it.
The company may sell Bitcoin or other assets to fund these payments, which is why it now says it must be free to sell as well as buy.
He declined to give a timeframe for his $100,000 target, saying he plans in centuries, not months.
Strategy’s longer-term forecast is for Bitcoin to grow 20% to 30% a year over the next two decades.

Friday’s upcoming MSCI decision on whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices is the nearest catalyst, since an exclusion could trigger passive selling of the shares even if Saylor plays down its importance.
On the positive side, regulatory guidance from US agencies has eased a key overhang.

Saylor argued that AI will reduce the value of companies built on large human workforces or on chasing the next breakthrough product, while increasing demand for scarce capital such as Palm Beach real estate, gold and Bitcoin.
In his words, investors will look for things robots cannot make more of.
By his own description, Bitcoin is also a volatile asset, with volatility of around 40, while Strategy’s shares run at roughly 80.
Saylor also defended Strategy’s sale of a small amount of Bitcoin in June, when prices were around $73,000, a move that unsettled the market.
Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy and listed under the ticker MSTR, started as an enterprise software company.
Since August 2020 it has focused on buying and holding Bitcoin, funded largely by issuing shares, debt and preferred-style securities.
It is now the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, with holdings Saylor puts at more than $70 billion.
If AI makes labour and software abundant, assets with fixed supply could gain relative appeal.

Bloomberg’s interviewers also challenged it, noting that AI is absorbing much of the market’s capital and that the scarcity rotation has yet to show clearly in Bitcoin, which remains about 30% below last year’s record high.
Fed's Williams sees no 2027 rate hike, diverging from trader bets as Bitcoin slips from $84k.
Saylor called the proposal a bad precedent, argued Strategy is an operating company like banks and insurers, and said the decision was not that important to the firm.
It would also set a precedent for the growing number of similar companies.
Saylor is talking his book, but his core pitch, that AI makes scarcity more valuable, is an argument worth weighing on its merits.

And what we established this summer is the ability for the company to buy and sell the credit, buy and sell the equity, and buy and sell the Bitcoin, and that was a big unlock for all of our investors and every asset class.”Strategy bought 250 BTC last week at an average price of $86,194 per Bitcoin, bringing its total to 848,250 BTC.

Strategy’s new willingness to sell Bitcoin as well as buy it removes the assumption that the largest corporate holder is a one-way buyer, adding a potential source of supply in weaker markets. On the positive side, regulatory guidance from US agencies has eased a key overhang. Bitcoin still has to compete for capital with AI stocks and with Treasury yields that have risen sharply this year, so a turn lower in yields after US inflation data would be the clearest macro tailwind for his $100,000 call. Saylor is talking his book, but his core pitch, that AI makes scarcity more valuable, is an argument worth weighing on its merits. Strategy co-founder and executive chairman Michael Saylor said Bitcoin is entering a new bull market and should climb back above $100,000, arguing that artificial intelligence will push investors towards assets whose supply cannot be expanded. Speaking to Bloomberg Television at DC Fintech Week on Tuesday, Saylor said Bitcoin bottomed slightly below $60,000 during the past year’s contraction and has since rebounded into the $80,000s. He declined to give a timeframe for his $100,000 target, saying he plans in centuries, not months. Strategy’s longer-term forecast is for Bitcoin to grow 20% to 30% a year over the next two decades. At the heart of his case is scarcity. Saylor argued that AI will reduce the value of companies built on large human workforces or on chasing the next breakthrough product, while increasing demand for scarce capital such as Palm Beach real estate, gold and Bitcoin. In his words, investors will look for things robots cannot make more of. The argument has some logic. If AI makes labour and software abundant, assets with fixed supply could gain relative appeal. But it comes from the executive chairman of the world’s largest corporate Bitcoin holder, with a stake he put at more than $70 billion. Bloomberg’s interviewers also challenged it, noting that AI is absorbing much of the market’s capital and that the scarcity rotation has yet to show clearly in Bitcoin, which remains about 30% below last year’s record high. Saylor countered that since Strategy began buying in August 2020, Bitcoin has returned about 38% a year and the company’s shares more than 50% a year, outpacing gold and every Magnificent Seven stock except Nvidia. By his own description, Bitcoin is also a volatile asset, with volatility of around 40, while Strategy’s shares run at roughly 80. He pointed to new tailwinds: favourable US regulation, faster bank adoption, the spread of tokenised securities and the growth of digital credit. He said the Senate’s failure to advance the Clarity Act was the best outcome for the industry, as guidance from the Treasury, the SEC and the CFTC proved more supportive than the bill’s restrictions. Saylor also defended Strategy’s sale of a small amount of Bitcoin in June, when prices were around $73,000, a move that unsettled the market. He described the company as a structured finance business that must be able to buy or sell Bitcoin, equity or credit as conditions require, mainly to support dividends on its credit products. He said those products pay 10% to 12% treated as a return of capital, which defers tax, and that the company expects to keep increasing its Bitcoin holdings in a bull market. MSCI is due to decide on Friday whether to exclude companies like Strategy from its global indices on the grounds they mainly accumulate assets. Saylor called the proposal a bad precedent, argued Strategy is an operating company like banks and insurers, and said the decision was not that important to the firm. Explainer: MSCI, Strategy and the index question What is MSCI? MSCI is one of the world’s largest index providers. Its benchmarks, such as the MSCI World and MSCI USA, are tracked by trillions of dollars in pension funds, ETFs and other investment products. When a company joins or leaves an MSCI index, funds that track it generally have to buy or sell the shares, whatever their view of the company. What is Strategy? Strategy, formerly MicroStrategy and listed under the ticker MSTR, started as an enterprise software company. Since August 2020 it has focused on buying and holding Bitcoin, funded largely by issuing shares, debt and preferred-style securities. It is now the largest corporate holder of Bitcoin, with holdings Saylor puts at more than $70 billion. What are “digital credit” products? These are Strategy’s income-paying securities, such as STRC, backed by the company’s Bitcoin holdings. Saylor says they pay 10% to 12% a year, treated as a return of capital, which generally defers tax rather than removing it. The company may sell Bitcoin or other assets to fund these payments, which is why it now says it must be free to sell as well as buy. What is MSCI considering? MSCI has been reviewing whether companies whose main activity is accumulating digital assets, often called digital asset treasury companies, should stay in its global equity indices. It is assessing whether these firms are operating businesses or are closer to investment vehicles, which index providers often exclude. Why does it matter? Exclusion could force index-tracking funds to sell Strategy shares, putting pressure on the stock and potentially on the company’s ability to raise money. It would also set a precedent for the growing number of similar companies. Saylor argues Strategy is an operating company comparable to banks and insurers, since it creates and sells credit products. He says the decision is not that important to the firm. What happens next? MSCI is due to announce its decision on Friday, October 16. A decision to exclude would typically take effect at a later index review, giving funds time to adjust. extraction.body: Footage of Kelly Clarkson's visit to Brooklyn novelty shop Art of Play, which she accused of giving her the "Pretty Woman" treatment , has surfaced online. On Tuesday evening, podcaster Pablo Torre posted security camera footage of Clarkson's visit to Art of Play on Saturday, where she said she was snubbed after inquiring about buying a $15,000 automaton bird named Molly. In the video, Clarkson is spotted wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow t-shirt and baggy jeans while looking around the store with her children. "The Voice" judge can be seen standing in front of the automaton bird in-question, before flagging down an employee. However, their conversation is not documented by the security footage. Later in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways, with the latter going on to assist another customer in the store. Clarkson goes on to speak with a different store employee, where she is seen gesturing and appears to be upset. Clarkson's visit at Art of Play lasted less than five minutes, per the video. This video footage marks the latest in the ongoing feud between Clarkson and the novelty store, whose owner Adam Rubin accused the singer of putting his employees "in danger" over the drama. "We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," he told Inside Edition. "Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It's just social warfare." He added: "When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations." A representative for Clarkson did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment. The drama all started on Saturday, when Clarkson took to X and accused a sales associate of looking at her "as if I couldn't afford" to shop there. "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," she wrote. "Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in 'Pretty Woman.' For sure, check it out." As countless fans began leaving negative reviews for Art of Play following Clarkson's post, the store pushed back on her narrative. "Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying 'Molly,' a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here," the owners explained on Sunday. "Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale." The statement added: "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." The back-and-forth didn't stop there, however. Clarkson doubled down on her criticism, writing in one pointed follow-up post: "So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. Got it." "Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," the pop star wrote on X . "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone 'yes, it's for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you'd like me to find something comparable for you I can.' That all never happened and now it's not for sale. Okay, cool." "And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things," she continued. "I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don't get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It's not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren't." passages: Footage of Kelly Clarkson's visit to Brooklyn novelty shop Art of Play, which she accused of giving her the "Pretty Woman" treatment , has surfaced online.

On Tuesday evening, podcaster Pablo Torre posted security camera footage of Clarkson's visit to Art of Play on Saturday, where she said she was snubbed after inquiring about buying a $15,000 automaton bird named Molly.

In the video, Clarkson is spotted wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow t-shirt and baggy jeans while looking around the store with her children. "The Voice" judge can be seen standing in front of the automaton bird in-question, before flagging down an employee. However, their conversation is not documented by the security footage.

Later in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways, with the latter going on to assist another customer in the store. Clarkson goes on to speak with a different store employee, where she is seen gesturing and appears to be upset. Clarkson's visit at Art of Play lasted less than five minutes, per the video.
This video footage marks the latest in the ongoing feud between Clarkson and the novelty store, whose owner Adam Rubin accused the singer of putting his employees "in danger" over the drama.
"We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," he told Inside Edition. "Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It's just social warfare."
He added: "When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations."
A representative for Clarkson did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment.
The drama all started on Saturday, when Clarkson took to X and accused a sales associate of looking at her "as if I couldn't afford" to shop there.

"Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," she wrote. "Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in 'Pretty Woman.' For sure, check it out."
As countless fans began leaving negative reviews for Art of Play following Clarkson's post, the store pushed back on her narrative.

"Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying 'Molly,' a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here," the owners explained on Sunday. "Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale."

The statement added: "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."
The back-and-forth didn't stop there, however. Clarkson doubled down on her criticism, writing in one pointed follow-up post: "So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. Got it."

"Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," the pop star wrote on X . "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone 'yes, it's for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you'd like me to find something comparable for you I can.' That all never happened and now it's not for sale. Okay, cool."

"And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things," she continued. "I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don't get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It's not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren't."

extraction.body: Footage of Kelly Clarkson's visit to Brooklyn novelty shop Art of Play, which she accused of giving her the "Pretty Woman" treatment , has surfaced online. On Tuesday evening, podcaster Pablo Torre posted security camera footage of Clarkson's visit to Art of Play on Saturday, where she said she was snubbed after inquiring about buying a $15,000 automaton bird named Molly. In the video, Clarkson is spotted wearing a baseball hat, bright yellow t-shirt and baggy jeans while looking around the store with her children. "The Voice" judge can be seen standing in front of the automaton bird in-question, before flagging down an employee. However, their conversation is not documented by the security footage. Later in the footage, Clarkson and the employee part ways, with the latter going on to assist another customer in the store. Clarkson goes on to speak with a different store employee, where she is seen gesturing and appears to be upset. Clarkson's visit at Art of Play lasted less than five minutes, per the video. This video footage marks the latest in the ongoing feud between Clarkson and the novelty store, whose owner Adam Rubin accused the singer of putting his employees "in danger" over the drama. "We are afraid for the safety of our shopkeepers. Kelly Clarkson has put us in danger," he told Inside Edition. "Things changed when she used her platform to attack us. It's just social warfare." He added: "When Kelly came in, the shop was crowded. She was dressed like everybody else in the shop. We treated her like a normal person, but apparently that did not live up to her expectations." A representative for Clarkson did not immediately respond to TheWrap's request for comment. The drama all started on Saturday, when Clarkson took to X and accused a sales associate of looking at her "as if I couldn't afford" to shop there. "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," she wrote. "Wow, dude. You're an idiot and just lost a huge sale. But y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts character in 'Pretty Woman.' For sure, check it out." As countless fans began leaving negative reviews for Art of Play following Clarkson's post, the store pushed back on her narrative. "Yesterday, Kelly Clarkson visited us in Brooklyn and inquired about buying 'Molly,' a one-of-a-kind singing and dancing bird automaton who plays an important role in the magic shows we host here," the owners explained on Sunday. "Molly is permanently attached to the wall and isn't for sale." The statement added: "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by 8 million people who have never visited our store. It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." The back-and-forth didn't stop there, however. Clarkson doubled down on her criticism, writing in one pointed follow-up post: "So you're not only rude, you're also a liar. Got it." "Cool, cool. Sure, it wasn't for sale. That's the narrative Art of Play is gonna go with," the pop star wrote on X . "So the whole conversation we had when I asked you if it was for sale whilst pointing to the price tag hanging on the wall with the title Singing Bird didn't happen as you elevator eyed me saying in a condescending tone 'yes, it's for sale but it costs 15,000 dollars so if you'd like me to find something comparable for you I can.' That all never happened and now it's not for sale. Okay, cool." "And by the way, I obviously support small businesses because I was literally at a small business trying to purchase things," she continued. "I love small businesses and know they are important and I always support them, but you don't get a free pass to treat people less than in your store just because you are a small business. It's not that hard to be kind. I never blast people but you my friend were an exception. Your store is really cool. Unfortunately, you aren't." extraction.body: Centrist Democrats in the Senate criticize Trump’s newfound billions, while working to boost the industry that enabled his grift. Donald Trump is cleaning up on crypto, recently disclosing a $1.4 billion windfall. Yet cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin have, after a year of flying high in the wake of Trump’s election, plummeted. The crypto industry is putting hopes for its revival in a long-awaited bill, under debate in the Senate, called the Clarity Act, which could open the doors to Wall Street investments. The result is that even crypto’s most staunch Democratic allies will find it hard to back a crypto wishlist like the Clarity Act, which will need support from at least seven Senate Democrats to overcome a filibuster. Take crypto stalwarts like centrist Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., the chair of the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, who issued a statement demanding that any crypto bill include ethics provisions to stop Trump’s crypto profiteering. With the industry poised to spend tens of millions more on the midterm elections , however, Gillibrand and other centrist Democrats may yet be tempted to sign off on window dressing instead of a crackdown, said crypto critics. “Sen. Gillibrand and too many of her colleagues prioritize and spend enormous time pushing crypto’s special interest agenda, which is to get legitimized by the weakest possible law and regulated by the smallest, most underfunded, least capable, and most capture-able financial regulator,” Dennis Kelleher, the CEO of the nonprofit Better Markets, said in a statement last Monday. “That is presumably because the crypto industry has spent hundreds of millions of dollars in campaigns to buy friends and attempt to get crypto’s special interest agenda enacted.” Gillibrand has dismissed those criticisms. In a statement of her own last week, she expressed her desire to both advance the bill and crack down on Trump. “We cannot let self-dealing destroy an opportunity to strengthen consumer protections, crack down on illicit finance, and expand economic opportunity for the millions of Americans our financial system has left behind,” Gillibrand said. “The time to act is now — and that must include ethics reforms that prohibit members of Congress, the president, and their spouses from cashing in on their office.” For crypto, the numbers are sobering. Bitcoin soared from roughly $60,000 just before Trump’s election to about twice that by October of last year. Since then, it and other digital assets have cratered. Bitcoin now trades back around $63,000 a token. The market’s gyrations did not stop Trump and his family members from profiting handsomely off the $TRUMP meme coin and other ventures. His roughly $1.4 billion of crypto profits last year meant that he cleared more than the largest publicly traded company in the industry, Coinbase, according to crypto commentator Scott Melker . The White House has defended Trump’s crypto windfall as legal, a point even his critics concede is likely true. Crypto’s fortunes now appear to hinge largely on whether Congress passes the Clarity Act, which is intended to create an overall regulatory framework for the industry. “If the bill passed, you would probably see a bump for the industry,” said Mark Hays, the associate director for cryptocurrency and financial technology at Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress. “So much of crypto rides on sentiment, and if the bill were passed and signed into law, you would likely see an increase in prices just based on that sentiment alone.” One sign of how much of the industry is placing its bets on Congress came in a recent quarterly earnings call held by Coinbase. Analysts asked the company’s executives several times how the Clarity Act would affect their bottom line. The company’s executives said that it could mean that Wall Street, which has been reluctant to dive headlong into the industry, will finally start to spend on crypto. Passing the law, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said , would “just unlock a lot of institutional capital that’ll flow into the space broadly.” Crypto needs to win over seven Democrats to beat a filibuster, or eight if Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., remains absent due to illness. Progressives such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., have expressed broad concerns that the law could lead to the next financial crash. Centrists like Gillibrand, meanwhile, have voiced narrower concerns. One of their biggest hang-ups with the legislation, they say, is the question of whether it will rein in Trump’s crypto ventures. Gillibrand occupies a powerful position in the party: She serves as the caucus’s top fundraiser as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. And she has positioned herself as a leader in Clarity Act negotiations, despite not serving on the relevant committees. Asked last month about the negotiations over the bill at the Aspen Ideas Festival — a cozy gathering of politicos and business executives in the Colorado mountain town — Gillibrand said she was working hard to overcome the ethics obstacle. “We’re working hand in glove with Republicans,” Gillibrand said . “We’re negotiating with staff from the White House so that everyone is clear about what the bill is going to say, and we’re going to do our best to land that plane.” Gillibrand’s public statements have repeatedly telegraphed her desire to see some version of the legislation passed. Gillibrand says it is urgent to get consumer protections on the books. Observers say the urgency may also be motivated by the industry’s massive campaign war chest . Over one-third of the corporate money spent on this year’s elections so far has come from the crypto industry, according to a recent report from the nonprofit watchdog group Public Citizen . That amounts to $189 million, including $82 million routed through a single industry super PAC called Fairshake , which is backed by Coinbase. Rick Claypool, the research director for Public Citizen’s president’s office, said that as chair of the DSCC, Gillibrand is keenly aware of crypto’s campaign spending potential. “I’m sure it’s top of mind,” Claypool told The Intercept. “Part of the whole goal of the corporate crypto spending is to make sure that lawmakers in general, but also in particular those who are in fundraising, leadership positions, think of the industry before they think of voters.” Other Democrats tipped as maybes on the bill include Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, who last month nudged other Democrats on the banking committee to vote for a draft of the bill, along with a swath of the caucus’s more centrist members. The final text of the bill has yet to drop, despite a promise from Bitcoin evangelist Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wy., that it would be released over the July 4 weekend. The industry’s deadlines for passing the law keep slipping. Its best chance may be to secure passage before the Senate leaves August 10 for an extended period of work in their home states. Hays said senators should ignore the industry’s artificial deadlines. His group recently released a poll suggesting that most voters are concerned about the crypto industry’s influence in Washington. “Yes, Democrats are looking over their shoulder, but I think they should be reading the room and saying, ‘Wait a second, is this really a priority?’” Hays said. “Or, is this the kind of pay-to-play politics that have gotten so many voters frustrated in the first place?” Correction: July 13, 2026, 8:59 a.m. ET An earlier version of this article stated that Donald Trump disclosed his $1.4 billion in income from crypto last week; it was disclosed on June 30. Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.” The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy. IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history. That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026? I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history. We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

sources.title: Sen. Gillibrand’s 22-year-old son raises $30M for trading startup as Dem champions crypto in DC - New York Post
passages: Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) — one of Capitol Hill’s most prominent boosters of cryptocurrency legislation — has reportedly raised $30 million to launch a derivatives exchange startup that is already valued at $300 million.

Theodore Gillibrand, whose mother has emerged as a leading advocate for crypto regulation and stablecoin legislation, secured the funding round for his startup, American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation, or APEC, Fortune reported.
“My son is a grown adult starting his own independent business,” Gillibrand said in a statement provided to The Post by her office.
Fortune noted that the crypto industry has also embraced perpetual futures, which have become increasingly popular among traders over the past year.

Theodore Gillibrand, whose mother has emerged as a leading advocate for crypto regulation and stablecoin legislation, secured the funding round for his startup, American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation, or APEC, Fortune reported. “My son is a grown adult starting his own independent business,” Gillibrand said in a statement provided to The Post by her office. “I have no involvement in it whatsoever. That said, I’m enormously proud of him and wish him nothing but the best.” The fundraising was led by venture capital firm Lux Capital, according to Fortune, which cited sources familiar with the matter. The deal values the startup at $300 million, the report said. APEC plans to offer perpetual futures contracts, known as “perps,” which allow traders to bet on the future price of assets without owning them and without the expiration dates attached to traditional futures contracts. “The American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation will be offering perpetual futures on US equities,” an APEC spokesperson told The Post. “There will be no cryptocurrencies on the platform and the platform is not built on blockchain technology.” According to a presentation filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company intends to seek approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to offer perpetual futures tied to equities and stock indexes rather than cryptocurrencies. “It is clear that the future of these markets is not in offshore and unregulated foreign entities but rather in a regulated and institutional American company,” Theodore Gillibrand said in a statement confirming details of the funding round, according to Fortune. The senatorial scion graduated from Stanford University on Sunday. His LinkedIn profile lists prior stints as a fellow at crypto-focused venture firm Paradigm and as an intern at Andreessen Horowitz, a major Silicon Valley investor with significant crypto holdings. His mother has spent years positioning herself as one of the cryptocurrency industry’s most influential Democratic allies in Washington. Gillibrand partnered with Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) on landmark legislation aimed at creating a federal framework for regulating digital assets and has argued that clear rules are needed to keep crypto innovation and jobs in the US. She was also a leading Democratic architect of the GENIUS Act, legislation establishing a regulatory framework for stablecoins. Fortune noted that the crypto industry has also embraced perpetual futures, which have become increasingly popular among traders over the past year. The growth of products such as perpetual futures has coincided with a broader push by regulators and lawmakers to bring more digital-asset-related trading activity under US oversight rather than leaving it to offshore exchanges. A spokesperson for Lux Capital confirmed to Fortune that the firm led the investment round.

sources.title: Kirsten Gillibrand, Crypto’s Favorite Democrat - New York Magazine
passages: Kirsten Gillibrand’s Labradoodle pressed himself against my legs, happily accepting scratches and offering up a stuffed animal he hoped I would tug from his mouth (I obliged).

New York’s junior senator, her once-blonde hair now closer to the white of Maple’s coat, then sat down across from me in her office, ready to explain how cryptocurrency had become one of her most prominent legislative priorities.
Gillibrand now finds herself in a crypto-related ethical morass that extends beyond her chief of staff’s remarks.
The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance.

When Gillibrand first became aware of crypto, she said, it looked to her like an answer to a problem she had spent years trying to solve: the roughly one in five New York households that are unbanked or underbanked.
Crypto appeared on Gillibrand’s radar not long after her presidential campaign fizzled out.
She said she first heard about it from constituents and financial regulators, then in hearings about cybercrime and illicit finance.
“In the early stages, nobody knew anything about it.
So I started reading some books and listening to podcasts and trying to understand what the industry was about,” she told me.
“Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me.
My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her.
“It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said.
Eighteen Senate Democrats, almost all of them recipients of crypto largesse, joined Republicans to pass the bill.
In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too.
And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity.

Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company.
Two decades ago, Gillibrand won election to the House as a right-leaning Democrat from a conservative upstate district.
Gillibrand is not only one of crypto’s most important Democratic allies but also chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, responsible for raising money for her colleagues.
The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC.
That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC.

This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried , who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally.
A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation.
This year, she played much the same role for the CLARITY Act, the crypto industry’s great unfinished legislative project, pressing fellow Democrats for their votes.

But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said.
A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well.
Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC.

extraction.body: Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section. At first, Maple was by my side. Kirsten Gillibrand’s Labradoodle pressed himself against my legs, happily accepting scratches and offering up a stuffed animal he hoped I would tug from his mouth (I obliged). New York’s junior senator, her once-blonde hair now closer to the white of Maple’s coat, then sat down across from me in her office, ready to explain how cryptocurrency had become one of her most prominent legislative priorities. It was not an obvious place for her to end up. Two decades ago, Gillibrand won election to the House as a right-leaning Democrat from a conservative upstate district. After her appointment to Hillary Clinton’s vacated Senate seat three years later, she moved sharply left , emerging as a leading voice against sexual assault in the military and on college campuses. At the height of the Me Too movement, she led the charge in calling for Senator Al Franken to resign, then ran for president in 2019 as a staunch progressive, describing some of her former positions as moral failings and warning against “circles and systems of power” sustained by “corruption and greed.” Today, she is the Democratic Party’s leading champion of an industry notorious for fraud, spectacular collapses, and scams — and the eye-watering sums it spends to win the favor of politicians in both parties. Crypto appeared on Gillibrand’s radar not long after her presidential campaign fizzled out. She said she first heard about it from constituents and financial regulators, then in hearings about cybercrime and illicit finance. “In the early stages, nobody knew anything about it. I didn’t know anything about it. So I started reading some books and listening to podcasts and trying to understand what the industry was about,” she told me. The more she learned, she said, the more frustrated she became that lawmakers seemed content to leave it alone. “What I was seeing from Congress is that they were too unwilling and unable to learn about a new industry and actually do the basic regulation,” she added. Before running for Congress, Gillibrand spent 15 years as a securities lawyer. “I was very knowledgeable about credit default swaps when most of my colleagues didn’t even know what a credit default swap was,” she explained. “Complex commercial issues that need to be regulated are something I’m just very familiar with, and it’s not scary for me.” In 2025, Gillibrand was the lead Democratic sponsor of the GENIUS Act, which laid down federal rules for stablecoins, or tokens designed to avoid the wild price swings of cryptocurrencies by pegging them to the U.S. dollar. Reporting at the time described her roaming the Senate floor with a binder, buttonholing skeptical Democrats, listening to their problems with the bill, and carrying their proposed changes back to Republican negotiators. Eighteen Senate Democrats, almost all of them recipients of crypto largesse, joined Republicans to pass the bill. This year, she played much the same role for the CLARITY Act, the crypto industry’s great unfinished legislative project, pressing fellow Democrats for their votes. The sweeping bill would have moved much of digital-asset trading out of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s securities-law regime and into a new framework overseen by the chronically underfunded and much weaker Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The previous SEC had sued major trading platforms, including Coinbase, Kraken, and Binance, only for the suits to be dropped once Trump was sworn in for a second term. This was “why CLARITY was so existential for the industry,” according to Amanda Fischer, who served as chief of staff in the Biden SEC. The bill would have “codified and blessed their business structures and protected past conduct from future enforcement.” It would also have made it easier for banks and other traditional financial firms to enter the crypto market, allowing them to trade, hold, lend against, and process payments in digital assets — an enormous step toward knitting the crypto industry into the traditional financial system. The bill appeared headed for passage until negotiations foundered over how to prevent elected officials from profiting from crypto, a newly urgent question given the Trump family’s budding crypto empire . When Republicans brought the bill to the floor without a bipartisan agreement on stronger ethics provisions, it became clear the bill would fail, and Gillibrand joined the rest of the Democratic caucus in voting “no.” Gillibrand is not only one of crypto’s most important Democratic allies but also chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, responsible for raising money for her colleagues. According to reporting by Punchbowl News , Gillibrand’s chief of staff, Jess Fassler, invoked his boss’s fundraising position while urging other Democratic aides to help advance the GENIUS Act, according to four aides present. Some took the remark as an implicit warning about the political consequences of crossing the industry. (Fassler denies making any threats.) Gillibrand now finds herself in a crypto-related ethical morass that extends beyond her chief of staff’s remarks. Her 22-year-old son, Theo, is the head of a start-up backed in part by crypto investors — including one who donates to his mother and the DSCC — that is seeking regulatory approval to bring a crypto-native trading product into conventional financial markets. Her campaign coffers are stuffed with crypto money, while former aides have rotated between her office and the industry. When I mentioned that her former communications director had made crypto purchases a week before she announced her first stab at crypto regulation, Gillibrand said she had “no lens on that at all.” Her office, she said, tells employees “to be good people and serve the state of New York and help people every day.” By then, Maple, who had spent the interview pressed against my legs, was barking at me. When Gillibrand first became aware of crypto, she said, it looked to her like an answer to a problem she had spent years trying to solve: the roughly one in five New York households that are unbanked or underbanked. Her attempts to authorize banking through the post office were being blocked by Republicans who opposed it as more big government and unfair competition for local banks. “One of the use cases of crypto that was brought to me very early when I started meeting with stakeholders — they’re like, ‘This democratizes finance,’” she said. Eventually, she concluded, “I could then accomplish what I was trying to accomplish with postal banking by highly regulating an industry that’s making banking available to everybody who doesn’t have a bank account.” In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too. Lummis was an enthusiast as well as an investor: She had first bought bitcoin in 2013 and purchased an additional $50,001 to $100,000 worth in August 2021, a transaction she disclosed late under the STOCK Act — the transparency law Gillibrand herself had sponsored. Gillibrand approached her. “Why don’t we write the regulation?” she remembered asking. “Why don’t we do the rules of the road? Because this industry has so much corruption, so much grift, so much wild west.” The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC. That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC. This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried , who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally. Gillibrand gave his donations to charity but drew the opposite lesson. For her, the spectacular failure of FTX was proof not that crypto should be kept at arm’s length but that Congress had waited too long to bring it under the umbrella of financial regulation. Gillibrand’s answer to nearly every criticism of crypto is that it makes regulation only more urgent, not less. “Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me. My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her. “It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said. “It’s like saying ‘Don’t regulate the internet.’” Crypto was, of course, being monitored and targeted by the SEC, but Gillibrand contended that many crypto tokens function more like commodities, hence making the CFTC a more appropriate regulator — which is what the industry argues as well. One of Gillibrand’s central rationales — that digital assets can bring the under- and unbanked into the financial system — has an obvious problem. Tonantzin Carmona, the director of economic policy at the Century Foundation who studies financial inclusion and cryptocurrency, noted that most ordinary consumers buy crypto through apps and exchanges that generally require a bank account or debit card. Crypto ATMs offer a cash work-around but can carry steep fees and have become fertile ground for scams. The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance. “In my opinion, the CLARITY Act was a financial crisis waiting to happen,” Lee Reiners, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official who teaches financial regulation at Duke University, told me. When FTX collapsed in 2022, the damage remained largely contained within crypto because digital assets still had relatively few connections to banks and traditional markets. CLARITY, Reiners argued, would have helped erase that separation: “Certainly, if CLARITY had passed, it would have supercharged the integration of crypto into the financial system.” At the same time, he said, the bill would have given the industry a “patina of regulation” — enough of a federal seal of approval to attract more customers and institutions without imposing the full set of rules that governs conventional securities firms. “The crypto industry wanted this bill to pass,” he said, “so they could point and say, ‘Look, we are regulated now. Come on in. The water’s warm and nice.’” Corey Frayer, who served as a senior adviser to former Biden SEC chair Gary Gensler and worked on crypto-asset policy, argued that the entire theory behind CLARITY was misguided. “The securities laws are not only about the business you’re offering,” Frayer told me. “The securities laws are primarily about how you raise money for that business.” If a company raises money from investors by promising them profits, he explained, it must comply with securities laws, including disclosure requirements, whether it’s developing a conventional product or a cryptocurrency. To him, the industry’s argument for different rules amounted to companies insisting they shouldn’t have to follow those laws because — he waved his hands — “technology.” He pointed to Coinbase, which combines functions that conventional finance generally separates: exchange, custody, clearing, and brokerage and venture investing. For an industry that talks frequently about democratizing finance, Frayer said, “the crypto market is actually far less democratic. It is far more concentrated, more run by powerful, concentrated interests than even the admittedly broken traditional markets.” Mark Hays, who specializes in cryptocurrency and financial technology for the nonprofits Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress, put it this way: “They just want to become your bank, your broker, and everything else under one roof — but without the same rules those entities have to agree to because we spent 100 years trying to keep them under regulatory check.” Gillibrand makes the opposite case: Tying stablecoins to cash and Treasuries under federal supervision makes the market safer, not more dangerous. “You don’t reduce systemic risk by pretending a market doesn’t exist,” one of her aides told me. Many of the fears about crypto ultimately depend on its becoming much bigger than it is today. “There’s all kinds of financial-stability implications, but they’re by and large premised on volume,” Allen said. “So if no one uses these things, then most of the risks are avoided.” This is a point on which the two sides agree, sort of. Gillibrand told me what she expects to happen with crypto if she gets the CLARITY Act through in the future. “Once it’s regulated,” she said, “people will be able to use it much more.” The industry would naturally also like that to happen. And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity. Donors to her 2024 reelection campaign included Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong; Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and chief legal officer Stuart Alderoty; Electric Capital co-founders Avichal Garg and Curtis Spencer; Solana co-founder Raj Gokal; Digital Currency Group executive Mark Murphy; and Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with their wives, Felicia Horowitz and Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen. After Gillibrand’s election, the money kept coming. Contributors to her campaign or affiliated committees since then have included Coinbase president Emilie Choi and chief policy officer Faryar Shirzad; Paradigm co-founder Fred Ehrsam and managing partner Alana Palmedo; Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse; Andreessen Horowitz crypto partner Chris Dixon; Kraken chairman Jesse Powell and co-CEO David Ripley; and Tyler Winklevoss, the Gemini co-founder and major crypto donor who, with his brother, Cameron, personally lobbied Trump against his first nominee to chair the CFTC, Brian Quintenz, helping derail his nomination. Trump instead installed Mike Selig, a former lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. In June, Gillibrand’s son Theo raised $30 million for a start-up called American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation. The fundraising round was led by Lux Capital — a shareholder of FTX before it collapsed — which valued the company at $300 million. One of Theo’s angel investors is Chris Larsen, the Ripple co-founder and Gillibrand donor. Although APEC is not a cryptocurrency exchange (it wants to offer perpetual futures on stocks and stock indexes, a type of highly leveraged derivative with no expiration date), the product came to prominence in crypto markets. These contracts provide no new capital to the companies whose shares they track. Instead, they offer traders another way to gamble on price swings, potentially magnifying losses and spreading them through the broader financial system — a familiar Wall Street arrangement in which the profits are private but the risks are everyone’s problem. Theo himself is a product of the crypto world. Before graduating from Stanford, he interned at Andreessen Horowitz and completed a fellowship at Paradigm. In May 2025, while his mother was helping push GENIUS through the Senate, he co-authored an article in a Stanford newspaper founded by Peter Thiel urging Congress to pass the bill, without disclosing his obvious connection to its lead Democratic sponsor. Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company. At Stanford, Baker said, a network of investors and scouts is on the lookout for teenagers who can be “quickly and heavily monetized.” APEC said Lux did not recruit Theo Gillibrand while he was at Stanford, but its success does depend heavily on a good relationship with regulators in Washington. The company has found open doors at Trump’s SEC and CFTC, the agencies that will determine whether and how its novel contracts can legally trade. Theo Gillibrand has said that CFTC officials were “very excited” by his proposals and that Trump’s financial regulators were more willing to listen than their predecessors had been. A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well. Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC. Andrew Siegel went from serving as general counsel at Galaxy, one of the country’s largest crypto firms, to a senior counsel job with Gillibrand. The revolving door is hardly unusual in Washington, but one case inside Gillibrand’s office raises a different question. Senior congressional staff are required to file financial-disclosure statements if they earn above a certain threshold. When I pulled those of Evan Lukaske, Gillibrand’s former communications director and the aide handling her crypto messaging, they indicated he had bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of bitcoin on March 9, 2022, and the same amount of ether eight days later. A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation. That bill — the first stab at what would eventually become known as CLARITY — specifically placed bitcoin and ether under CFTC commodity regulation, and Lukaske served as a spokesman defending it when it was unveiled that June. Lukaske did not respond to questions about what he knew when he made the trades or whether he was acting on nonpublic information. Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics at Democracy Defenders Fund and a former federal-government ethics official, stopped short of saying those trades establish wrongdoing. But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said. Either way, “the timing raises serious concerns.” I asked Gillibrand whether she had ever given her staff guidance about trading cryptocurrency. “No,” she said, “we don’t involve ourselves with our staff at all about what they own and what they have.” Would she have a problem with staff members buying crypto while she was working on legislation that could benefit the industry?

The bill appeared headed for passage until negotiations foundered over how to prevent elected officials from profiting from crypto, a newly urgent question given the Trump family’s budding crypto empire . When Republicans brought the bill to the floor without a bipartisan agreement on stronger ethics provisions, it became clear the bill would fail, and Gillibrand joined the rest of the Democratic caucus in voting “no.”

Gillibrand is not only one of crypto’s most important Democratic allies but also chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, responsible for raising money for her colleagues. According to reporting by Punchbowl News , Gillibrand’s chief of staff, Jess Fassler, invoked his boss’s fundraising position while urging other Democratic aides to help advance the GENIUS Act, according to four aides present. Some took the remark as an implicit warning about the political consequences of crossing the industry. (Fassler denies making any threats.)

Gillibrand now finds herself in a crypto-related ethical morass that extends beyond her chief of staff’s remarks. Her 22-year-old son, Theo, is the head of a start-up backed in part by crypto investors — including one who donates to his mother and the DSCC — that is seeking regulatory approval to bring a crypto-native trading product into conventional financial markets. Her campaign coffers are stuffed with crypto money, while former aides have rotated between her office and the industry. When I mentioned that her former communications director had made crypto purchases a week before she announced her first stab at crypto regulation, Gillibrand said she had “no lens on that at all.” Her office, she said, tells employees “to be good people and serve the state of New York and help people every day.”
By then, Maple, who had spent the interview pressed against my legs, was barking at me.

When Gillibrand first became aware of crypto, she said, it looked to her like an answer to a problem she had spent years trying to solve: the roughly one in five New York households that are unbanked or underbanked. Her attempts to authorize banking through the post office were being blocked by Republicans who opposed it as more big government and unfair competition for local banks. “One of the use cases of crypto that was brought to me very early when I started meeting with stakeholders — they’re like, ‘This democratizes finance,’” she said. Eventually, she concluded, “I could then accomplish what I was trying to accomplish with postal banking by highly regulating an industry that’s making banking available to everybody who doesn’t have a bank account.”

In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too. Lummis was an enthusiast as well as an investor: She had first bought bitcoin in 2013 and purchased an additional $50,001 to $100,000 worth in August 2021, a transaction she disclosed late under the STOCK Act — the transparency law Gillibrand herself had sponsored. Gillibrand approached her. “Why don’t we write the regulation?” she remembered asking. “Why don’t we do the rules of the road? Because this industry has so much corruption, so much grift, so much wild west.”

The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC. That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC. This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried , who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally. Gillibrand gave his donations to charity but drew the opposite lesson. For her, the spectacular failure of FTX was proof not that crypto should be kept at arm’s length but that Congress had waited too long to bring it under the umbrella of financial regulation.

Gillibrand’s answer to nearly every criticism of crypto is that it makes regulation only more urgent, not less. “Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me. My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her. “It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said. “It’s like saying ‘Don’t regulate the internet.’” Crypto was, of course, being monitored and targeted by the SEC, but Gillibrand contended that many crypto tokens function more like commodities, hence making the CFTC a more appropriate regulator — which is what the industry argues as well.

One of Gillibrand’s central rationales — that digital assets can bring the under- and unbanked into the financial system — has an obvious problem. Tonantzin Carmona, the director of economic policy at the Century Foundation who studies financial inclusion and cryptocurrency, noted that most ordinary consumers buy crypto through apps and exchanges that generally require a bank account or debit card. Crypto ATMs offer a cash work-around but can carry steep fees and have become fertile ground for scams.

The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance. “In my opinion, the CLARITY Act was a financial crisis waiting to happen,” Lee Reiners, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official who teaches financial regulation at Duke University, told me. When FTX collapsed in 2022, the damage remained largely contained within crypto because digital assets still had relatively few connections to banks and traditional markets. CLARITY, Reiners argued, would have helped erase that separation: “Certainly, if CLARITY had passed, it would have supercharged the integration of crypto into the financial system.” At the same time, he said, the bill would have given the industry a “patina of regulation” — enough of a federal seal of approval to attract more customers and institutions without imposing the full set of rules that governs conventional securities firms. “The crypto industry wanted this bill to pass,” he said, “so they could point and say, ‘Look, we are regulated now. Come on in. The water’s warm and nice.’”

Corey Frayer, who served as a senior adviser to former Biden SEC chair Gary Gensler and worked on crypto-asset policy, argued that the entire theory behind CLARITY was misguided. “The securities laws are not only about the business you’re offering,” Frayer told me. “The securities laws are primarily about how you raise money for that business.” If a company raises money from investors by promising them profits, he explained, it must comply with securities laws, including disclosure requirements, whether it’s developing a conventional product or a cryptocurrency. To him, the industry’s argument for different rules amounted to companies insisting they shouldn’t have to follow those laws because — he waved his hands — “technology.” He pointed to Coinbase, which combines functions that conventional finance generally separates: exchange, custody, clearing, and brokerage and venture investing. For an industry that talks frequently about democratizing finance, Frayer said, “the crypto market is actually far less democratic. It is far more concentrated, more run by powerful, concentrated interests than even the admittedly broken traditional markets.”

Mark Hays, who specializes in cryptocurrency and financial technology for the nonprofits Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress, put it this way: “They just want to become your bank, your broker, and everything else under one roof — but without the same rules those entities have to agree to because we spent 100 years trying to keep them under regulatory check.”

Gillibrand makes the opposite case: Tying stablecoins to cash and Treasuries under federal supervision makes the market safer, not more dangerous. “You don’t reduce systemic risk by pretending a market doesn’t exist,” one of her aides told me.

Many of the fears about crypto ultimately depend on its becoming much bigger than it is today. “There’s all kinds of financial-stability implications, but they’re by and large premised on volume,” Allen said. “So if no one uses these things, then most of the risks are avoided.”
This is a point on which the two sides agree, sort of. Gillibrand told me what she expects to happen with crypto if she gets the CLARITY Act through in the future.
“Once it’s regulated,” she said, “people will be able to use it much more.”

The industry would naturally also like that to happen. And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity. Donors to her 2024 reelection campaign included Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong; Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and chief legal officer Stuart Alderoty; Electric Capital co-founders Avichal Garg and Curtis Spencer; Solana co-founder Raj Gokal; Digital Currency Group executive Mark Murphy; and Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with their wives, Felicia Horowitz and Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen.

After Gillibrand’s election, the money kept coming. Contributors to her campaign or affiliated committees since then have included Coinbase president Emilie Choi and chief policy officer Faryar Shirzad; Paradigm co-founder Fred Ehrsam and managing partner Alana Palmedo; Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse; Andreessen Horowitz crypto partner Chris Dixon; Kraken chairman Jesse Powell and co-CEO David Ripley; and Tyler Winklevoss, the Gemini co-founder and major crypto donor who, with his brother, Cameron, personally lobbied Trump against his first nominee to chair the CFTC, Brian Quintenz, helping derail his nomination. Trump instead installed Mike Selig, a former lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets.

In June, Gillibrand’s son Theo raised $30 million for a start-up called American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation. The fundraising round was led by Lux Capital — a shareholder of FTX before it collapsed — which valued the company at $300 million. One of Theo’s angel investors is Chris Larsen, the Ripple co-founder and Gillibrand donor. Although APEC is not a cryptocurrency exchange (it wants to offer perpetual futures on stocks and stock indexes, a type of highly leveraged derivative with no expiration date), the product came to prominence in crypto markets. These contracts provide no new capital to the companies whose shares they track. Instead, they offer traders another way to gamble on price swings, potentially magnifying losses and spreading them through the broader financial system — a familiar Wall Street arrangement in which the profits are private but the risks are everyone’s problem.

Theo himself is a product of the crypto world. Before graduating from Stanford, he interned at Andreessen Horowitz and completed a fellowship at Paradigm. In May 2025, while his mother was helping push GENIUS through the Senate, he co-authored an article in a Stanford newspaper founded by Peter Thiel urging Congress to pass the bill, without disclosing his obvious connection to its lead Democratic sponsor.

Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company. At Stanford, Baker said, a network of investors and scouts is on the lookout for teenagers who can be “quickly and heavily monetized.” APEC said Lux did not recruit Theo Gillibrand while he was at Stanford, but its success does depend heavily on a good relationship with regulators in Washington. The company has found open doors at Trump’s SEC and CFTC, the agencies that will determine whether and how its novel contracts can legally trade. Theo Gillibrand has said that CFTC officials were “very excited” by his proposals and that Trump’s financial regulators were more willing to listen than their predecessors had been.

A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well. Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC. Andrew Siegel went from serving as general counsel at Galaxy, one of the country’s largest crypto firms, to a senior counsel job with Gillibrand. The revolving door is hardly unusual in Washington, but one case inside Gillibrand’s office raises a different question.

Senior congressional staff are required to file financial-disclosure statements if they earn above a certain threshold. When I pulled those of Evan Lukaske, Gillibrand’s former communications director and the aide handling her crypto messaging, they indicated he had bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of bitcoin on March 9, 2022, and the same amount of ether eight days later. A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation. That bill — the first stab at what would eventually become known as CLARITY — specifically placed bitcoin and ether under CFTC commodity regulation, and Lukaske served as a spokesman defending it when it was unveiled that June. Lukaske did not respond to questions about what he knew when he made the trades or whether he was acting on nonpublic information.

Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics at Democracy Defenders Fund and a former federal-government ethics official, stopped short of saying those trades establish wrongdoing. But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said. Either way, “the timing raises serious concerns.”

I asked Gillibrand whether she had ever given her staff guidance about trading cryptocurrency. “No,” she said, “we don’t involve ourselves with our staff at all about what they own and what they have.”
Would she have a problem with staff members buying crypto while she was working on legislation that could benefit the industry?
