extraction.body: Centrist Democrats in the Senate criticize Trump’s newfound billions, while working to boost the industry that enabled his grift. Donald Trump is cleaning up on crypto, recently disclosing a $1.4 billion windfall. Yet cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin have, after a year of flying high in the wake of Trump’s election, plummeted. The crypto industry is putting hopes for its revival in a long-awaited bill, under debate in the Senate, called the Clarity Act, which could open the doors to Wall Street investments. The result is that even crypto’s most staunch Democratic allies will find it hard to back a crypto wishlist like the Clarity Act, which will need support from at least seven Senate Democrats to overcome a filibuster. Take crypto stalwarts like centrist Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., the chair of the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee, who issued a statement demanding that any crypto bill include ethics provisions to stop Trump’s crypto profiteering. With the industry poised to spend tens of millions more on the midterm elections , however, Gillibrand and other centrist Democrats may yet be tempted to sign off on window dressing instead of a crackdown, said crypto critics. “Sen. Gillibrand and too many of her colleagues prioritize and spend enormous time pushing crypto’s special interest agenda, which is to get legitimized by the weakest possible law and regulated by the smallest, most underfunded, least capable, and most capture-able financial regulator,” Dennis Kelleher, the CEO of the nonprofit Better Markets, said in a statement last Monday. “That is presumably because the crypto industry has spent hundreds of millions of dollars in campaigns to buy friends and attempt to get crypto’s special interest agenda enacted.” Gillibrand has dismissed those criticisms. In a statement of her own last week, she expressed her desire to both advance the bill and crack down on Trump. “We cannot let self-dealing destroy an opportunity to strengthen consumer protections, crack down on illicit finance, and expand economic opportunity for the millions of Americans our financial system has left behind,” Gillibrand said. “The time to act is now — and that must include ethics reforms that prohibit members of Congress, the president, and their spouses from cashing in on their office.” For crypto, the numbers are sobering. Bitcoin soared from roughly $60,000 just before Trump’s election to about twice that by October of last year. Since then, it and other digital assets have cratered. Bitcoin now trades back around $63,000 a token. The market’s gyrations did not stop Trump and his family members from profiting handsomely off the $TRUMP meme coin and other ventures. His roughly $1.4 billion of crypto profits last year meant that he cleared more than the largest publicly traded company in the industry, Coinbase, according to crypto commentator Scott Melker . The White House has defended Trump’s crypto windfall as legal, a point even his critics concede is likely true. Crypto’s fortunes now appear to hinge largely on whether Congress passes the Clarity Act, which is intended to create an overall regulatory framework for the industry. “If the bill passed, you would probably see a bump for the industry,” said Mark Hays, the associate director for cryptocurrency and financial technology at Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress. “So much of crypto rides on sentiment, and if the bill were passed and signed into law, you would likely see an increase in prices just based on that sentiment alone.” One sign of how much of the industry is placing its bets on Congress came in a recent quarterly earnings call held by Coinbase. Analysts asked the company’s executives several times how the Clarity Act would affect their bottom line. The company’s executives said that it could mean that Wall Street, which has been reluctant to dive headlong into the industry, will finally start to spend on crypto. Passing the law, Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said , would “just unlock a lot of institutional capital that’ll flow into the space broadly.” Crypto needs to win over seven Democrats to beat a filibuster, or eight if Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., remains absent due to illness. Progressives such as Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., have expressed broad concerns that the law could lead to the next financial crash. Centrists like Gillibrand, meanwhile, have voiced narrower concerns. One of their biggest hang-ups with the legislation, they say, is the question of whether it will rein in Trump’s crypto ventures. Gillibrand occupies a powerful position in the party: She serves as the caucus’s top fundraiser as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. And she has positioned herself as a leader in Clarity Act negotiations, despite not serving on the relevant committees. Asked last month about the negotiations over the bill at the Aspen Ideas Festival — a cozy gathering of politicos and business executives in the Colorado mountain town — Gillibrand said she was working hard to overcome the ethics obstacle. “We’re working hand in glove with Republicans,” Gillibrand said . “We’re negotiating with staff from the White House so that everyone is clear about what the bill is going to say, and we’re going to do our best to land that plane.” Gillibrand’s public statements have repeatedly telegraphed her desire to see some version of the legislation passed. Gillibrand says it is urgent to get consumer protections on the books. Observers say the urgency may also be motivated by the industry’s massive campaign war chest . Over one-third of the corporate money spent on this year’s elections so far has come from the crypto industry, according to a recent report from the nonprofit watchdog group Public Citizen . That amounts to $189 million, including $82 million routed through a single industry super PAC called Fairshake , which is backed by Coinbase. Rick Claypool, the research director for Public Citizen’s president’s office, said that as chair of the DSCC, Gillibrand is keenly aware of crypto’s campaign spending potential. “I’m sure it’s top of mind,” Claypool told The Intercept. “Part of the whole goal of the corporate crypto spending is to make sure that lawmakers in general, but also in particular those who are in fundraising, leadership positions, think of the industry before they think of voters.” Other Democrats tipped as maybes on the bill include Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and Ruben Gallego of Arizona, who last month nudged other Democrats on the banking committee to vote for a draft of the bill, along with a swath of the caucus’s more centrist members. The final text of the bill has yet to drop, despite a promise from Bitcoin evangelist Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wy., that it would be released over the July 4 weekend. The industry’s deadlines for passing the law keep slipping. Its best chance may be to secure passage before the Senate leaves August 10 for an extended period of work in their home states. Hays said senators should ignore the industry’s artificial deadlines. His group recently released a poll suggesting that most voters are concerned about the crypto industry’s influence in Washington. “Yes, Democrats are looking over their shoulder, but I think they should be reading the room and saying, ‘Wait a second, is this really a priority?’” Hays said. “Or, is this the kind of pay-to-play politics that have gotten so many voters frustrated in the first place?” Correction: July 13, 2026, 8:59 a.m. ET An earlier version of this article stated that Donald Trump disclosed his $1.4 billion in income from crypto last week; it was disclosed on June 30. extraction.body: See more of our coverage in your search results. The 22-year-old son of Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) — one of Capitol Hill’s most prominent boosters of cryptocurrency legislation — has reportedly raised $30 million to launch a derivatives exchange startup that is already valued at $300 million. Theodore Gillibrand, whose mother has emerged as a leading advocate for crypto regulation and stablecoin legislation, secured the funding round for his startup, American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation, or APEC, Fortune reported. “My son is a grown adult starting his own independent business,” Gillibrand said in a statement provided to The Post by her office. “I have no involvement in it whatsoever. That said, I’m enormously proud of him and wish him nothing but the best.” The fundraising was led by venture capital firm Lux Capital, according to Fortune, which cited sources familiar with the matter. The deal values the startup at $300 million, the report said. APEC plans to offer perpetual futures contracts, known as “perps,” which allow traders to bet on the future price of assets without owning them and without the expiration dates attached to traditional futures contracts. “The American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation will be offering perpetual futures on US equities,” an APEC spokesperson told The Post. “There will be no cryptocurrencies on the platform and the platform is not built on blockchain technology.” According to a presentation filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company intends to seek approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to offer perpetual futures tied to equities and stock indexes rather than cryptocurrencies. “It is clear that the future of these markets is not in offshore and unregulated foreign entities but rather in a regulated and institutional American company,” Theodore Gillibrand said in a statement confirming details of the funding round, according to Fortune. The senatorial scion graduated from Stanford University on Sunday. His LinkedIn profile lists prior stints as a fellow at crypto-focused venture firm Paradigm and as an intern at Andreessen Horowitz, a major Silicon Valley investor with significant crypto holdings. His mother has spent years positioning herself as one of the cryptocurrency industry’s most influential Democratic allies in Washington. Gillibrand partnered with Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.) on landmark legislation aimed at creating a federal framework for regulating digital assets and has argued that clear rules are needed to keep crypto innovation and jobs in the US. She was also a leading Democratic architect of the GENIUS Act, legislation establishing a regulatory framework for stablecoins. extraction.body: Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section. At first, Maple was by my side. Kirsten Gillibrand’s Labradoodle pressed himself against my legs, happily accepting scratches and offering up a stuffed animal he hoped I would tug from his mouth (I obliged). New York’s junior senator, her once-blonde hair now closer to the white of Maple’s coat, then sat down across from me in her office, ready to explain how cryptocurrency had become one of her most prominent legislative priorities. It was not an obvious place for her to end up. Two decades ago, Gillibrand won election to the House as a right-leaning Democrat from a conservative upstate district. After her appointment to Hillary Clinton’s vacated Senate seat three years later, she moved sharply left , emerging as a leading voice against sexual assault in the military and on college campuses. At the height of the Me Too movement, she led the charge in calling for Senator Al Franken to resign, then ran for president in 2019 as a staunch progressive, describing some of her former positions as moral failings and warning against “circles and systems of power” sustained by “corruption and greed.” Today, she is the Democratic Party’s leading champion of an industry notorious for fraud, spectacular collapses, and scams — and the eye-watering sums it spends to win the favor of politicians in both parties. Crypto appeared on Gillibrand’s radar not long after her presidential campaign fizzled out. She said she first heard about it from constituents and financial regulators, then in hearings about cybercrime and illicit finance. “In the early stages, nobody knew anything about it. I didn’t know anything about it. So I started reading some books and listening to podcasts and trying to understand what the industry was about,” she told me. The more she learned, she said, the more frustrated she became that lawmakers seemed content to leave it alone. “What I was seeing from Congress is that they were too unwilling and unable to learn about a new industry and actually do the basic regulation,” she added. Before running for Congress, Gillibrand spent 15 years as a securities lawyer. “I was very knowledgeable about credit default swaps when most of my colleagues didn’t even know what a credit default swap was,” she explained. “Complex commercial issues that need to be regulated are something I’m just very familiar with, and it’s not scary for me.” In 2025, Gillibrand was the lead Democratic sponsor of the GENIUS Act, which laid down federal rules for stablecoins, or tokens designed to avoid the wild price swings of cryptocurrencies by pegging them to the U.S. dollar. Reporting at the time described her roaming the Senate floor with a binder, buttonholing skeptical Democrats, listening to their problems with the bill, and carrying their proposed changes back to Republican negotiators. Eighteen Senate Democrats, almost all of them recipients of crypto largesse, joined Republicans to pass the bill. This year, she played much the same role for the CLARITY Act, the crypto industry’s great unfinished legislative project, pressing fellow Democrats for their votes. The sweeping bill would have moved much of digital-asset trading out of the Securities and Exchange Commission’s securities-law regime and into a new framework overseen by the chronically underfunded and much weaker Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The previous SEC had sued major trading platforms, including Coinbase, Kraken, and Binance, only for the suits to be dropped once Trump was sworn in for a second term. This was “why CLARITY was so existential for the industry,” according to Amanda Fischer, who served as chief of staff in the Biden SEC. The bill would have “codified and blessed their business structures and protected past conduct from future enforcement.” It would also have made it easier for banks and other traditional financial firms to enter the crypto market, allowing them to trade, hold, lend against, and process payments in digital assets — an enormous step toward knitting the crypto industry into the traditional financial system. The bill appeared headed for passage until negotiations foundered over how to prevent elected officials from profiting from crypto, a newly urgent question given the Trump family’s budding crypto empire . When Republicans brought the bill to the floor without a bipartisan agreement on stronger ethics provisions, it became clear the bill would fail, and Gillibrand joined the rest of the Democratic caucus in voting “no.” Gillibrand is not only one of crypto’s most important Democratic allies but also chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, responsible for raising money for her colleagues. According to reporting by Punchbowl News , Gillibrand’s chief of staff, Jess Fassler, invoked his boss’s fundraising position while urging other Democratic aides to help advance the GENIUS Act, according to four aides present. Some took the remark as an implicit warning about the political consequences of crossing the industry. (Fassler denies making any threats.) Gillibrand now finds herself in a crypto-related ethical morass that extends beyond her chief of staff’s remarks. Her 22-year-old son, Theo, is the head of a start-up backed in part by crypto investors — including one who donates to his mother and the DSCC — that is seeking regulatory approval to bring a crypto-native trading product into conventional financial markets. Her campaign coffers are stuffed with crypto money, while former aides have rotated between her office and the industry. When I mentioned that her former communications director had made crypto purchases a week before she announced her first stab at crypto regulation, Gillibrand said she had “no lens on that at all.” Her office, she said, tells employees “to be good people and serve the state of New York and help people every day.” By then, Maple, who had spent the interview pressed against my legs, was barking at me. When Gillibrand first became aware of crypto, she said, it looked to her like an answer to a problem she had spent years trying to solve: the roughly one in five New York households that are unbanked or underbanked. Her attempts to authorize banking through the post office were being blocked by Republicans who opposed it as more big government and unfair competition for local banks. “One of the use cases of crypto that was brought to me very early when I started meeting with stakeholders — they’re like, ‘This democratizes finance,’” she said. Eventually, she concluded, “I could then accomplish what I was trying to accomplish with postal banking by highly regulating an industry that’s making banking available to everybody who doesn’t have a bank account.” In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too. Lummis was an enthusiast as well as an investor: She had first bought bitcoin in 2013 and purchased an additional $50,001 to $100,000 worth in August 2021, a transaction she disclosed late under the STOCK Act — the transparency law Gillibrand herself had sponsored. Gillibrand approached her. “Why don’t we write the regulation?” she remembered asking. “Why don’t we do the rules of the road? Because this industry has so much corruption, so much grift, so much wild west.” The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC. That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC. This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried , who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally. Gillibrand gave his donations to charity but drew the opposite lesson. For her, the spectacular failure of FTX was proof not that crypto should be kept at arm’s length but that Congress had waited too long to bring it under the umbrella of financial regulation. Gillibrand’s answer to nearly every criticism of crypto is that it makes regulation only more urgent, not less. “Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me. My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her. “It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said. “It’s like saying ‘Don’t regulate the internet.’” Crypto was, of course, being monitored and targeted by the SEC, but Gillibrand contended that many crypto tokens function more like commodities, hence making the CFTC a more appropriate regulator — which is what the industry argues as well. One of Gillibrand’s central rationales — that digital assets can bring the under- and unbanked into the financial system — has an obvious problem. Tonantzin Carmona, the director of economic policy at the Century Foundation who studies financial inclusion and cryptocurrency, noted that most ordinary consumers buy crypto through apps and exchanges that generally require a bank account or debit card. Crypto ATMs offer a cash work-around but can carry steep fees and have become fertile ground for scams. The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance. “In my opinion, the CLARITY Act was a financial crisis waiting to happen,” Lee Reiners, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official who teaches financial regulation at Duke University, told me. When FTX collapsed in 2022, the damage remained largely contained within crypto because digital assets still had relatively few connections to banks and traditional markets. CLARITY, Reiners argued, would have helped erase that separation: “Certainly, if CLARITY had passed, it would have supercharged the integration of crypto into the financial system.” At the same time, he said, the bill would have given the industry a “patina of regulation” — enough of a federal seal of approval to attract more customers and institutions without imposing the full set of rules that governs conventional securities firms. “The crypto industry wanted this bill to pass,” he said, “so they could point and say, ‘Look, we are regulated now. Come on in. The water’s warm and nice.’” Corey Frayer, who served as a senior adviser to former Biden SEC chair Gary Gensler and worked on crypto-asset policy, argued that the entire theory behind CLARITY was misguided. “The securities laws are not only about the business you’re offering,” Frayer told me. “The securities laws are primarily about how you raise money for that business.” If a company raises money from investors by promising them profits, he explained, it must comply with securities laws, including disclosure requirements, whether it’s developing a conventional product or a cryptocurrency. To him, the industry’s argument for different rules amounted to companies insisting they shouldn’t have to follow those laws because — he waved his hands — “technology.” He pointed to Coinbase, which combines functions that conventional finance generally separates: exchange, custody, clearing, and brokerage and venture investing. For an industry that talks frequently about democratizing finance, Frayer said, “the crypto market is actually far less democratic. It is far more concentrated, more run by powerful, concentrated interests than even the admittedly broken traditional markets.” Mark Hays, who specializes in cryptocurrency and financial technology for the nonprofits Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress, put it this way: “They just want to become your bank, your broker, and everything else under one roof — but without the same rules those entities have to agree to because we spent 100 years trying to keep them under regulatory check.” Gillibrand makes the opposite case: Tying stablecoins to cash and Treasuries under federal supervision makes the market safer, not more dangerous. “You don’t reduce systemic risk by pretending a market doesn’t exist,” one of her aides told me. Many of the fears about crypto ultimately depend on its becoming much bigger than it is today. “There’s all kinds of financial-stability implications, but they’re by and large premised on volume,” Allen said. “So if no one uses these things, then most of the risks are avoided.” This is a point on which the two sides agree, sort of. Gillibrand told me what she expects to happen with crypto if she gets the CLARITY Act through in the future. “Once it’s regulated,” she said, “people will be able to use it much more.” The industry would naturally also like that to happen. And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity. Donors to her 2024 reelection campaign included Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong; Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and chief legal officer Stuart Alderoty; Electric Capital co-founders Avichal Garg and Curtis Spencer; Solana co-founder Raj Gokal; Digital Currency Group executive Mark Murphy; and Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with their wives, Felicia Horowitz and Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen. After Gillibrand’s election, the money kept coming. Contributors to her campaign or affiliated committees since then have included Coinbase president Emilie Choi and chief policy officer Faryar Shirzad; Paradigm co-founder Fred Ehrsam and managing partner Alana Palmedo; Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse; Andreessen Horowitz crypto partner Chris Dixon; Kraken chairman Jesse Powell and co-CEO David Ripley; and Tyler Winklevoss, the Gemini co-founder and major crypto donor who, with his brother, Cameron, personally lobbied Trump against his first nominee to chair the CFTC, Brian Quintenz, helping derail his nomination. Trump instead installed Mike Selig, a former lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. In June, Gillibrand’s son Theo raised $30 million for a start-up called American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation. The fundraising round was led by Lux Capital — a shareholder of FTX before it collapsed — which valued the company at $300 million. One of Theo’s angel investors is Chris Larsen, the Ripple co-founder and Gillibrand donor. Although APEC is not a cryptocurrency exchange (it wants to offer perpetual futures on stocks and stock indexes, a type of highly leveraged derivative with no expiration date), the product came to prominence in crypto markets. These contracts provide no new capital to the companies whose shares they track. Instead, they offer traders another way to gamble on price swings, potentially magnifying losses and spreading them through the broader financial system — a familiar Wall Street arrangement in which the profits are private but the risks are everyone’s problem. Theo himself is a product of the crypto world. Before graduating from Stanford, he interned at Andreessen Horowitz and completed a fellowship at Paradigm. In May 2025, while his mother was helping push GENIUS through the Senate, he co-authored an article in a Stanford newspaper founded by Peter Thiel urging Congress to pass the bill, without disclosing his obvious connection to its lead Democratic sponsor. Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company. At Stanford, Baker said, a network of investors and scouts is on the lookout for teenagers who can be “quickly and heavily monetized.” APEC said Lux did not recruit Theo Gillibrand while he was at Stanford, but its success does depend heavily on a good relationship with regulators in Washington. The company has found open doors at Trump’s SEC and CFTC, the agencies that will determine whether and how its novel contracts can legally trade. Theo Gillibrand has said that CFTC officials were “very excited” by his proposals and that Trump’s financial regulators were more willing to listen than their predecessors had been. A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well. Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC. Andrew Siegel went from serving as general counsel at Galaxy, one of the country’s largest crypto firms, to a senior counsel job with Gillibrand. The revolving door is hardly unusual in Washington, but one case inside Gillibrand’s office raises a different question. Senior congressional staff are required to file financial-disclosure statements if they earn above a certain threshold. When I pulled those of Evan Lukaske, Gillibrand’s former communications director and the aide handling her crypto messaging, they indicated he had bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of bitcoin on March 9, 2022, and the same amount of ether eight days later. A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation. That bill — the first stab at what would eventually become known as CLARITY — specifically placed bitcoin and ether under CFTC commodity regulation, and Lukaske served as a spokesman defending it when it was unveiled that June. Lukaske did not respond to questions about what he knew when he made the trades or whether he was acting on nonpublic information. Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics at Democracy Defenders Fund and a former federal-government ethics official, stopped short of saying those trades establish wrongdoing. But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said. Either way, “the timing raises serious concerns.” I asked Gillibrand whether she had ever given her staff guidance about trading cryptocurrency. “No,” she said, “we don’t involve ourselves with our staff at all about what they own and what they have.” Would she have a problem with staff members buying crypto while she was working on legislation that could benefit the industry?

Her attempts to authorize banking through the post office were being blocked by Republicans who opposed it as more big government and unfair competition for local banks. “One of the use cases of crypto that was brought to me very early when I started meeting with stakeholders — they’re like, ‘This democratizes finance,’” she said. Eventually, she concluded, “I could then accomplish what I was trying to accomplish with postal banking by highly regulating an industry that’s making banking available to everybody who doesn’t have a bank account.”

In 2022, Gillibrand heard that Cynthia Lummis, a Republican senator from Wyoming, wanted to work on crypto regulation too. Lummis was an enthusiast as well as an investor: She had first bought bitcoin in 2013 and purchased an additional $50,001 to $100,000 worth in August 2021, a transaction she disclosed late under the STOCK Act — the transparency law Gillibrand herself had sponsored. Gillibrand approached her. “Why don’t we write the regulation?” she remembered asking. “Why don’t we do the rules of the road? Because this industry has so much corruption, so much grift, so much wild west.”

The same year, Gillibrand and Lummis introduced the Responsible Financial Innovation Act, which attempted to divide regulatory authority over crypto assets between the SEC and the CFTC. That September, Gillibrand also co-sponsored a bill handing oversight of crypto spot markets, where digital assets are bought and sold for immediate delivery, to the CFTC. This was the legislation Sam Bankman-Fried , who had donated to Gillibrand that June, was lobbying for so aggressively it became widely known as the “SBF bill.” When FTX collapsed months later, many Democrats rushed to distance themselves from Bankman-Fried and crypto generally. Gillibrand gave his donations to charity but drew the opposite lesson. For her, the spectacular failure of FTX was proof not that crypto should be kept at arm’s length but that Congress had waited too long to bring it under the umbrella of financial regulation.

Gillibrand’s answer to nearly every criticism of crypto is that it makes regulation only more urgent, not less. “Why would you allow a trillion-plus-dollar industry to go around allowing people to buy and sell shit and not regulate it?” she asked me. My suggestion that Congress might be better off refusing to legitimize the industry exasperated her. “It’s such an uneducated perspective,” she said. “It’s like saying ‘Don’t regulate the internet.’” Crypto was, of course, being monitored and targeted by the SEC, but Gillibrand contended that many crypto tokens function more like commodities, hence making the CFTC a more appropriate regulator — which is what the industry argues as well.

One of Gillibrand’s central rationales — that digital assets can bring the under- and unbanked into the financial system — has an obvious problem. Tonantzin Carmona, the director of economic policy at the Century Foundation who studies financial inclusion and cryptocurrency, noted that most ordinary consumers buy crypto through apps and exchanges that generally require a bank account or debit card. Crypto ATMs offer a cash work-around but can carry steep fees and have become fertile ground for scams.

The greater concern is what happens if Gillibrand succeeds in making crypto easier to use and more deeply embedded in ordinary finance. “In my opinion, the CLARITY Act was a financial crisis waiting to happen,” Lee Reiners, a former Federal Reserve Bank of New York official who teaches financial regulation at Duke University, told me. When FTX collapsed in 2022, the damage remained largely contained within crypto because digital assets still had relatively few connections to banks and traditional markets. CLARITY, Reiners argued, would have helped erase that separation: “Certainly, if CLARITY had passed, it would have supercharged the integration of crypto into the financial system.” At the same time, he said, the bill would have given the industry a “patina of regulation” — enough of a federal seal of approval to attract more customers and institutions without imposing the full set of rules that governs conventional securities firms. “The crypto industry wanted this bill to pass,” he said, “so they could point and say, ‘Look, we are regulated now. Come on in. The water’s warm and nice.’”

Corey Frayer, who served as a senior adviser to former Biden SEC chair Gary Gensler and worked on crypto-asset policy, argued that the entire theory behind CLARITY was misguided. “The securities laws are not only about the business you’re offering,” Frayer told me. “The securities laws are primarily about how you raise money for that business.” If a company raises money from investors by promising them profits, he explained, it must comply with securities laws, including disclosure requirements, whether it’s developing a conventional product or a cryptocurrency. To him, the industry’s argument for different rules amounted to companies insisting they shouldn’t have to follow those laws because — he waved his hands — “technology.” He pointed to Coinbase, which combines functions that conventional finance generally separates: exchange, custody, clearing, and brokerage and venture investing. For an industry that talks frequently about democratizing finance, Frayer said, “the crypto market is actually far less democratic. It is far more concentrated, more run by powerful, concentrated interests than even the admittedly broken traditional markets.”

Mark Hays, who specializes in cryptocurrency and financial technology for the nonprofits Americans for Financial Reform and Demand Progress, put it this way: “They just want to become your bank, your broker, and everything else under one roof — but without the same rules those entities have to agree to because we spent 100 years trying to keep them under regulatory check.”

Gillibrand makes the opposite case: Tying stablecoins to cash and Treasuries under federal supervision makes the market safer, not more dangerous. “You don’t reduce systemic risk by pretending a market doesn’t exist,” one of her aides told me.

Many of the fears about crypto ultimately depend on its becoming much bigger than it is today. “There’s all kinds of financial-stability implications, but they’re by and large premised on volume,” Allen said. “So if no one uses these things, then most of the risks are avoided.”
This is a point on which the two sides agree, sort of. Gillibrand told me what she expects to happen with crypto if she gets the CLARITY Act through in the future.
“Once it’s regulated,” she said, “people will be able to use it much more.”

The industry would naturally also like that to happen. And Gillibrand has benefited greatly from big crypto’s generosity. Donors to her 2024 reelection campaign included Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong; Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and chief legal officer Stuart Alderoty; Electric Capital co-founders Avichal Garg and Curtis Spencer; Solana co-founder Raj Gokal; Digital Currency Group executive Mark Murphy; and Andreessen Horowitz co-founders Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, along with their wives, Felicia Horowitz and Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen.

After Gillibrand’s election, the money kept coming. Contributors to her campaign or affiliated committees since then have included Coinbase president Emilie Choi and chief policy officer Faryar Shirzad; Paradigm co-founder Fred Ehrsam and managing partner Alana Palmedo; Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse; Andreessen Horowitz crypto partner Chris Dixon; Kraken chairman Jesse Powell and co-CEO David Ripley; and Tyler Winklevoss, the Gemini co-founder and major crypto donor who, with his brother, Cameron, personally lobbied Trump against his first nominee to chair the CFTC, Brian Quintenz, helping derail his nomination. Trump instead installed Mike Selig, a former lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets.

In June, Gillibrand’s son Theo raised $30 million for a start-up called American Perpetuals Exchange Corporation. The fundraising round was led by Lux Capital — a shareholder of FTX before it collapsed — which valued the company at $300 million. One of Theo’s angel investors is Chris Larsen, the Ripple co-founder and Gillibrand donor. Although APEC is not a cryptocurrency exchange (it wants to offer perpetual futures on stocks and stock indexes, a type of highly leveraged derivative with no expiration date), the product came to prominence in crypto markets. These contracts provide no new capital to the companies whose shares they track. Instead, they offer traders another way to gamble on price swings, potentially magnifying losses and spreading them through the broader financial system — a familiar Wall Street arrangement in which the profits are private but the risks are everyone’s problem.

Theo himself is a product of the crypto world. Before graduating from Stanford, he interned at Andreessen Horowitz and completed a fellowship at Paradigm. In May 2025, while his mother was helping push GENIUS through the Senate, he co-authored an article in a Stanford newspaper founded by Peter Thiel urging Congress to pass the bill, without disclosing his obvious connection to its lead Democratic sponsor.

Theo Baker, a Stanford classmate of Theo Gillibrand’s and the author of a recent book about the university’s relationship with Silicon Valley, offers a perspective on how a 22-year-old with the right last name ends up running a $300 million crypto-inspired finance company. At Stanford, Baker said, a network of investors and scouts is on the lookout for teenagers who can be “quickly and heavily monetized.” APEC said Lux did not recruit Theo Gillibrand while he was at Stanford, but its success does depend heavily on a good relationship with regulators in Washington. The company has found open doors at Trump’s SEC and CFTC, the agencies that will determine whether and how its novel contracts can legally trade. Theo Gillibrand has said that CFTC officials were “very excited” by his proposals and that Trump’s financial regulators were more willing to listen than their predecessors had been.

A crypto ecosystem has developed around Senator Gillibrand’s office as well. Before joining Gillibrand’s staff and working on crypto legislation, Dorothy DeWitt worked at Coinbase, then ran a division of the CFTC. Andrew Siegel went from serving as general counsel at Galaxy, one of the country’s largest crypto firms, to a senior counsel job with Gillibrand. The revolving door is hardly unusual in Washington, but one case inside Gillibrand’s office raises a different question.

Senior congressional staff are required to file financial-disclosure statements if they earn above a certain threshold. When I pulled those of Evan Lukaske, Gillibrand’s former communications director and the aide handling her crypto messaging, they indicated he had bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of bitcoin on March 9, 2022, and the same amount of ether eight days later. A week later, Gillibrand announced she and Lummis were writing comprehensive crypto legislation. That bill — the first stab at what would eventually become known as CLARITY — specifically placed bitcoin and ether under CFTC commodity regulation, and Lukaske served as a spokesman defending it when it was unveiled that June. Lukaske did not respond to questions about what he knew when he made the trades or whether he was acting on nonpublic information.

Chris Swartz, senior counsel and deputy director of ethics at Democracy Defenders Fund and a former federal-government ethics official, stopped short of saying those trades establish wrongdoing. But, he said, Gillibrand’s staffers “should have known that purchasing crypto might create at least the appearance of impropriety.” Whether Lukaske’s purchases were “simply inadvisably timed trades or suggest use of nonpublic information for private gain is a question of fact that would have to be looked into,” Swartz said. Either way, “the timing raises serious concerns.”

I asked Gillibrand whether she had ever given her staff guidance about trading cryptocurrency. “No,” she said, “we don’t involve ourselves with our staff at all about what they own and what they have.”
Would she have a problem with staff members buying crypto while she was working on legislation that could benefit the industry?

(NASDAQ: NEOV ) (“NeoVolta” or the “Company”), a U.S.-based energy technology company delivering scalable energy storage solutions, today announced that its majority-owned subsidiary, NeoVolta Power, LLC (“NeoVolta Power”), has entered into a binding capacity reservation agreement with Infinite Grid Capital (“IGC”) to provide battery energy storage system (“BESS”) equipment for North Ontario Edge artificial intelligence datacenter (“Edge AIDC”) projects for calendar year 2027. Today’s announcement represents the first major commercial commitment under NeoVolta Power’s previously announced utility-scale framework with IGC, which contemplates approximately 1.1 GWh of potential BESS deployments and approximately $200 million of potential supply across multiple markets. The approximately $53M binding commitment advances the Company’s strategy of converting early utility-scale demand visibility into binding commercial relationships as its Pendergrass manufacturing platform progresses through commissioning and production-ramp activities. “This is an important commercial milestone for NeoVolta Power and a meaningful validation of the platform we have built at Pendergrass,” said Ardes Johnson, Chief Executive Officer of NeoVolta. “The project demonstrates how our BESS manufacturing, a differentiated supply-chain strategy, and scalable energy-storage products can address the rapidly growing power-infrastructure needs of data centers and other energy-intensive customers. As we advance the production ramp at Pendergrass, our focus is on executing this initial commitment and converting additional qualified demand into binding customer orders.” The capacity reservation agreement is intended to support the Northern Ontario Edge AIDC project and represents an initial commercial step within NeoVolta’s broader relationship with IGC. The relationship was previously announced as a non-binding framework spanning approximately 1.1 GWh of potential demand. The Company believes the initial data-center-related commitment is strategically significant. The commitment provides commercial validation for NeoVolta Power’s utility-scale product offering and its domestic BESS manufacturing strategy. NeoVolta will host a grand-opening ceremony for its NeoVolta Power facility in Pendergrass, Georgia, later today. Members of NeoVolta management, key strategic partners, media, and local officials are expected to attend. The event marks the official opening of the Company’s 210,600-square-foot facility, a purpose-built domestic BESS manufacturing platform designed to assemble commercial, industrial, and utility-scale energy-storage products. NeoVolta expects to provide additional updates regarding the commissioning process, manufacturing milestones, and commercial activity as appropriate. IGC focuses on building reliable and flexible energy assets that ensure continuous power for AI workloads, industrial operations, and other mission-critical facilities. extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. extraction.body: Your vibe-coded applications can now be easily run on Android smartphones without having to first go public on the Google Play Store, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. A new feature will allow users to launch their own personal apps on their device via Google Play using their standard Google account, but they will remain completely private. These personal apps won’t show up in Google Play’s search or listing pages, and won’t be shared with anyone except for the app’s creator. The idea comes as more people are experimenting with building their own applications via AI for specific, personal needs. However, being able to use that app on their own Android device has meant publishing to Google Play, making it accessible to the Play Store’s some 3 billion users. That led many to limit their vibe-coding efforts to web apps that could run on any device instead of something built natively for Android. Now, Google says Android device owners can vibe-code an app using Google AI Studio, then launch it for their own use. These apps are still required to comply with Google Play’s existing policies but allow users to experiment more directly with building apps for Android. Initially, the feature will be available to users in the U.S., age 18 and up. “That’s why the future of apps on Google Play is personal, secure, and built by everyone — and it’s why Play is leading the charge and moving from ‘there’s an app for that’ to ‘there’s an app for me,’” said Sam Bright, Google’s VP and GM for the Google Play and Developer Ecosystem, in a press briefing ahead of Tuesday’s launch. “We started Google Play with a simple goal: to connect you with the apps you love. But after today, we hope it’s clear: Play has evolved to become so much more than that.” In the months ahead, the company said that users will be able to share their vibe-coded creations with a network of trusted friends. That means the apps you built for family or friends, or maybe your child’s T-ball league, could be used with a small group of people, without having to go public on the Play Store. And if the app ever really becomes popular, there will be a way to shift the personal app to one that’s published on the Google Play Store for everyone to try, after completing the trust and safety reviews. Google will also allow users to curate their own lists of games, post questions about games to a new Community Posts section, and join new 48-hour gaming challenges called Sprints, among other gaming-related feature updates. Plus, the Play Store’s built-in AI assistant, Ask Play, is being updated to offer comparisons, allowing users to see the key differences between similar applications. Google Play apps and games will also be more deeply integrated into Gemini’s conversations. The changes are rolling out alongside Google Play’s new support for an age-range feature that allows parents to share their child’s age range, but not their exact birthdate, with developers to get an age-appropriate experience. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15. Flox makes edge devices that process data on-site rather than in the cloud. Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior. A motion sensor wakes the device when it detects movement, triggering a camera that uses on-device models to identify nearby animals. The device then emits a species-appropriate sound to scare them away. Nozkova says the system learns from experience, too, and varies its responses so animals don’t get habituated to repeated signals. The company currently sells battery-operated devices that can be mounted on poles, trees, and other structures. It also offers a software platform that shows clients where the devices are deployed and what’s happening on the ground. The platform can also generate reports for regulatory compliance and for uses like biodiversity monitoring. The longer-term goal is to make the software portable enough to run on machines that work outside, including trains, cars, and drones. Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations. The company sells edge units up front, then charges an annual software and AI subscription after the first year. Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains. Train manufacturer Alstom is one such partner. The company expects to end 2026 with revenue of about $1.5 million, Nozkova said. As unique as Flox’s product and approach are, the startup is not without competition. Robin Radar’s Scarecrow also uses species-specific distress calls to disperse birds and it records the activity, while iCHASE sells a system that detects birds with computer vision and targets them with a moving laser, adjusting its response as needed. Nozkova says her moat is the breadth of the system and the data Flox has collected in the field, which she calls “ground truth on what actually makes a moose or a grizzly bear move safely.” “Physical AI is walking out of the factory and into the messy, alive outdoors,” Nozkova says. “Every machine that operates outside — trains, trucks, drones, tractors, robots — will need to understand nature, and nature intelligence is the next layer of the perception stack. Almost nobody is building it.” The company has raised about $5 million across pre-seed and seed rounds so far, with the seed round led by Unconventional Ventures and Tilia Impact Ventures. Co-investors across the rounds include GENIUS NY, Norrsken, Satgana, and angel investors, Nozkova said. The company is now opening a $10 million Series A, which would mostly go toward growing from about 150 devices to several thousand deployed units and extending the underlying system beyond its current wildlife use cases. He covered North American and European M&A, equity, regulatory news and debt markets at Reuters and Acuris Global, and has also written about travel, tourism, entertainment and books. sources.title: Sweden's Flox Intelligence raises €2.5 million to become a “digital shepherd” guiding wildlife away from danger - EU-Startups
passages: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America.
It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds.
The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language.
“For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on.
For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead?

“Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist.

The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform.
This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid.
Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin.
It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm.
The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US.
It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses.
Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise.
It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months.
Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime.

Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure.

Sara Nozkova , CEO and co-founder of Flox Intelligence, said, “The future of infrastructure safety will include wildlife intelligence by default. “For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on. For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead? “Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist. Our goal is to make wildlife intelligence a standard layer of modern operations — and to lead that category globally.” Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

coreStoryFacts.text: Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.
Like autonomous vehicles, they use perception systems to sense their surroundings, but theirs are trained on wildlife behavior.

Nozkova says about 150 Flox devices are live in North America, Europe, and Australia at airfields and airport perimeters, road and rail corridors (especially fence ends and crossings along wildlife corridors), national parks, agricultural land, urban areas, mining sites, and critical infrastructure such as electrical substations.
The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs.

After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.
Flox also has OEM partnerships with companies that pay an annual fee to deploy its software on vehicles, like trains.

extraction.body: When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks. The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet. The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays. Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure. “I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent,” she told TechCrunch. After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation. “We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them,” she said. “Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.” So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is. sources.title: Sweden's Flox Intelligence raises €2.5 million to become a “digital shepherd” guiding wildlife away from danger - EU-Startups
passages: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America.
It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds.
The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language.
“For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on.
For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead?

“Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist.

The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform.
This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid.
Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin.
It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm.
The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US.
It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses.
Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise.
It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months.
Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime.

Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure.

extraction.body: Flox Intelligence , a wildlife intelligence company building AI systems enabling infrastructure to prevent human-wildlife conflict, today announced a €2.5 million ($3 million) Seed+ round to accelerate deployments across North America. The round was led by Tilia Impact Ventures, with participation from Satgana, GENIUS NY (operated by CenterState CEO), J.O.S.S. and existing investors Unconventional Ventures and Almi Invest. Sara Nozkova , CEO and co-founder of Flox Intelligence, said, “The future of infrastructure safety will include wildlife intelligence by default. “For decades, we’ve relied on reactive tools — from scare tactics to fences — that don’t scale, don’t learn, and don’t protect the corridors wildlife depends on. For so many years, we have been fighting wildlife, but what if we could communicate with them instead? “Flox Intelligence is building a future where critical infrastructure can proactively prevent conflict, where animal movement is respected and safer, and where people and wildlife can finally coexist. Our goal is to make wildlife intelligence a standard layer of modern operations — and to lead that category globally.” Flox Intelligence was founded in 2020 by Nozkova and Tomas Becklin. It was born out of an AI research lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. The company recently relocated its commercial headquarters to the US. Flox Intelligence is an AI-powered wildlife intelligence company that aims to create a world where humans and wildlife coexist. According to the company, it builds autonomous systems deployed on the edge that guide wildlife in real time using AI, bioacoustics, and applied wildlife science. The technology prevents collisions, damage, and disruption across critical infrastructure, including railways, airports, roads, agriculture, and industrial sites, and provides reporting through the Flox Wildlife Platform. The company claims to replace reactive, fragmented deterrents like scarecrows, pyrotechnics, gunshots, and fences with a modern, autonomous layer of prevention and learning at the edge. Every deployment makes the next one smarter, and collectively, these deployments are building one of the world’s largest non-lethal wildlife datasets and windows into how wildlife moves, adapts, and survives alongside human infrastructure. Flox Intelligence mentions that human-wildlife conflict is already a global multi-billion-euro problem. This keeps growing every year as humans take more space, wild animals are pushed closer to urban spaces, and transportation systems get faster, quieter, and harder to avoid. According to the company, existing tools do not scale and lack adaptive learning capabilities. Flox Intelligence claims to be built on a different premise. It is building edge-based physical AI that can operate 24/7 in harsh environments, where decisions have to be made in seconds. The company combines embedded systems, real-time sensing, and applied wildlife science to speak with animals in their own language. “In other words, it turns wildlife communication into actionable intelligence — enabling critical infrastructure to “speak” with wildlife and gently guide them away from high-risk zones before incidents happen,” mentioned Flox Intelligence. The startup’s first commercial product, Edge, is an intelligent wildlife deterrent system built for harsh, real-world environments, engineered for multiple species, extreme weather, remote sites, limited connectivity, and long uptime. It is always on, multi-species, multi-modal, and deployed at the edge. Flox Intelligence has already started shipping Edge pods to the front lines of human-wildlife conflict, including airports dealing with coyotes, deer, and bird strike risks, to rail corridors affected by large wildlife such as moose and bears. It is also helping DOT road networks where deer and bison collisions drive injuries, fatalities, and financial losses. Some other use cases of Edge include ranches and farms balancing predator-healthy ecosystems with livestock protection, and cities and public spaces that witness wildlife movement. The company reports that Edge has logged over 60,000 wildlife events across 27 species, and early deployments show measurable reductions in wildlife presence in high-risk zones. This funding follows Flox Intelligence’s Seed round in July last year. It has expanded its operations across the U.S. and Canada, grown its New York headquarters, and accelerated commercial deployments over the past few months. The fresh capital will be used by the company to accelerate deployments across North America. It will also support growing international demand for Flox Intelligence’s AI-powered wildlife deterrence platform across airports, rail corridors, road networks, and industrial sites. Flox Intelligence reports that it already works with major airports, departments of transportation, infrastructure owners, and mission-driven partners across North America and Europe. Its partners include the U.S. Department of Agriculture, GRR Gerald R. Ford International Airport, WWF, KWS Group, Boliden, and Alstom.

passages: Instead of a store of its own, Apple relies on a system similar to CarPlay in the car.
Third-party apps run on the paired iPhone or iPad and are merely displayed on HomeView.
According to Apple, the display supports “compatible third-party audio and video apps” from the iPhone.
According to a Wired report cited by 9to5Mac , developers can use their existing CarPlay apps for this.
An Apple display, but no apps to download: Apple’s new smart home display, HomeView, comes without its own App Store, Apple confirmed to MacRumors .
Even before the unveiling, Mark Gurman of Bloomberg had reported that developers would be left out of HomeView for now.
The Apple blogger Stephen Hackett calls the approach “weird” on his blog, 512 Pixels.
He doubts that HomeView will push developers to put more effort into CarPlay.
At the same time, he sees HomeView as a successful combination of building blocks Apple users already know, held together by the iPhone, iCloud and Continuity.
The advantage for users: Anyone who already has CarPlay apps on their iPhone does not need to install anything extra on HomeView.
For Europe, the question does not arise for now anyway.
HomeView will not be sold in the European Union because Siri AI on iOS is currently not available in the E.U., as Apple said at launch .
Apple blames the Digital Markets Act, saying it would otherwise have to give any virtual assistant direct access to users’ private data and the ability to control other apps.
Amazon has opened its Echo Show displays to third parties for years through Alexa skills, and Google’s Nest Hub can play content from numerous apps via Chromecast.
Only Apple’s own apps come preinstalled, including Music, Podcasts, News, Calendar, FaceTime and Messages.
Apple has not announced a developer kit specifically for HomeView.
