WASHINGTON — In just ten days, the Army will activate Project Gatekeeper, a new AI-enhanced cybersecurity sandbox designed to vet commercial software for use on Army networks, officials announced today. Launching Oct. 23, Project Gatekeeper is creating a single sandboxed environment — running on the Army’s cloud but isolated from operationa l networks and sensitive data — where companies can bring their software for assessment, even if they don’t have an Army contract or a program manager to sponsor them. Officials say Gatekeeper will cut the time required to get software approved fro m months to “minutes” — without sacrificing security in the process. “Success, to me, looks like a company, within minutes, is able to log in, submit their code and get the green check mark from our pipeline that says you are good to go,” acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabe Chiulli told reporters at the annual AUSA conference here this morning. Compare that with the current, cumbersome clearance process that can take days or weeks — stalling some software projects for as long as nine months, Chiulli and other officials said. That’s a long time to wait for a software upgrade, especially under a process that officials say lack consistent cybersecurity practices, transparency for contractors and visibility for Army leaders into what’s actually happening on their networks. “We have had to do a lot of weird janky things to get code into our environments,” Chiulli said. Sometimes, he said, “I’m not sure how they’re getting code over to us.” The root of the problem, officials said, is that the Army has lacked a single, standardized, centralized process for bringing commercial software onto its secure networks. Instead, “it was up to every program manager,” explained David Markowitz, the service’s chief data and analytics officer. But many program offices lacked the capability or willingness to conduct cybersecurity assessments of new and unfamiliar code. Rather than evaluate the software themselves, they would wait for another organization to vet the company and officially grant its software Authority To Operate (ATO) on military networks. “A lot of times, organizations in the Army won’t talk to [companies] until they have this ‘golden ATO,’” Chiulli said. That created a kind of Catch-22 : The companies best positioned to win Army software contracts where often the ones that already had them. Meanwhile new, innovative entrants — the kind of companies that the Pentagon’s been courting for over a decade — struggled to navigate the combined complexities of cybersecurity rules, procurement regulations and Army bureaucracy. If a program manager did decide to give a new piece of software a chance, moreover, they rarely had a dedicated, isolated sand box in which t o test it. Instead, they had to bring it onto an Army network and assess it there. That, in turn, required the company’s personnel to get cleared for Common Access Cards (CAC) so they could access the Army system. “We spent a lot of time and energy trying to get people CAC cards simply to help work with us,” Chiulli said. “This is to get rid of all that [and] lower barriers to entry.” Gatekeeper will let companies test their software before they have an Army contract, a program manager sponsoring them or even a formal request for proposals to respond to, the officials emphasized, allowing prospective vendors to identify and address cybersecurity problems before trying to do business with the service. Companies will still need CAC cards to access the platform initially, officials acknowledged. But the Army is finalizing an agreement with the General Services Administration (GSA) to use its Login.gov platform, which allows secure access to government systems for members of the public. “We’re looking at mid-November to have that integrated, at which point we’ll be able to make this actually commercially accessible,” said David Wright, chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center (ASIC). Once a company gets access to the Gatekeeper platfor m, it can upload its software and run it through the Army’s standardized cybersecurity tools, including an AI assessment, offi cials explained. In minutes, the automated system will either tell the company its software passed the test or give detailed, actionable feedback explaining why it failed. Gatekeeper will also include the Army’s DevSecOps software development kit, Wright said, giving companies a secure environment in which to address problems using tools the Army itself has vetted. “The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements,” Wright emphasized, “but more to make the process more accessible and available, so that they can get immediate feedback and understand what it is that needs to be adjusted or corrected before these things are brought into an Army environment.”

The Army has resorted to "weird janky things" to move software into its systems, he said. At times, officials could not readily determine how code had been transferred. Under previous arrangements, companies often had to establish access to government infrastructure and learn Army security practices before they could demonstrate a product. Officials said some program offices were reluctant to consider vendors that did not already have an Authority to Operate, effectively favoring companies with existing government relationships. The initiative follows a broader Army effort to cut acquisition red tape and bring commercial technology to soldiers faster , which military leaders outlined earlier this year. Gatekeeper is intended to replace those arrangements with a standardized testing process that lets developers identify vulnerabilities and correct them before moving software toward use on Army networks. At launch, Gatekeeper will still require a Common Access Card, or CAC, the military credential that outside developers have often needed to work on government systems. Chiulli said the Army has sometimes issued those cards to entire teams of civilian developers simply to allow them to transfer software. "Sometimes companies have a hundred developers in the back end that are not necessarily going to have CAC cards," Chiulli said. "And sometimes we give all those people CAC cards simply so that they can do it and commit to us." David Wright, a chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center, said the service expects to integrate the General Services Administration's Login.gov system by mid-November. That would make Gatekeeper accessible to commercial developers without military credentials. Officials estimated that 40 to 50 companies are already encountering obstacles Gatekeeper is designed to address. The Army has also worked with defense startups through its xTech program , supporting projects involving AI-enabled sensors, predictive maintenance and other emerging technologies. The platform will provide an isolated environment, separated from operational Army networks, where developers can upload software for conventional cybersecurity screening and an AI-assisted review. Officials estimated that 40 to 50 companies are already encountering obstacles Gatekeeper is designed to address. The Army has also worked with defense startups through its xTech program , supporting projects involving AI-enabled sensors, predictive maintenance and other emerging technologies.
The platform will provide an isolated environment, separated from operational Army networks, where developers can upload software for conventional cybersecurity screening and an AI-assisted review.

Officials said companies could receive feedback within minutes, correct identified problems and resubmit their code. The system uses established Army software security pipelines, including tools already used by other military services. Passing the scans would not, by itself, grant final authorization to operate on military networks.
During the roundtable, Military.com asked how much money and manpower the Army expects to save by reducing the need to issue CACs to civilian developers.
"I don't know what that number is," Chiulli said, declining to offer an arbitrary estimate.
Wright said the workload is spread among numerous program offices, making it difficult to calculate the time spent arranging credentials for outside contractors.
"I know that subjectively it feels like the answer is a lot," Wright said.

David M. Markowitz, the Army's deputy chief information officer and chief data and analytics officer, said some major software programs can take six to eight months before developers have an initial working capability. He added that larger programs can cost millions of dollars per month.
Those expenses reflect broader software development efforts, not the specific cost of issuing CACs. Officials did not provide an estimate of Gatekeeper's potential savings.

The Army is also working through how it will protect companies' proprietary code, particularly when they submit software before securing government contracts. Wright described nondisclosure agreements and controls to keep different vendors' code separate, but said some arrangements remain unresolved.

Officials maintained that faster access would not reduce cybersecurity standards. The effort comes amid broader Pentagon investments in cybersecurity and moves toward more consistent security requirements for defense contractors under the fiscal 2026 defense legislation.
Whether Gatekeeper delivers the promised efficiencies will become clearer after the wider commercial rollout, which the Army is targeting for November.

extraction.body: The service’s new cybersecurity testing sandbox will stand up on Oct. 23, said acting Army CIO Gabe Chiulli, streamlining the current cumbersome, ad hoc arrangements for clearing commercial software for Army networks. WASHINGTON — In just ten days, the Army will activate Project Gatekeeper, a new AI-enhanced cybersecurity sandbox designed to vet commercial software for use on Army networks, officials announced today. Launching Oct. 23, Project Gatekeeper is creating a single sandboxed environment — running on the Army’s cloud but isolated from operationa l networks and sensitive data — where companies can bring their software for assessment, even if they don’t have an Army contract or a program manager to sponsor them. Officials say Gatekeeper will cut the time required to get software approved fro m months to “minutes” — without sacrificing security in the process. “Success, to me, looks like a company, within minutes, is able to log in, submit their code and get the green check mark from our pipeline that says you are good to go,” acting Army Chief Information Officer Gabe Chiulli told reporters at the annual AUSA conference here this morning. Compare that with the current, cumbersome clearance process that can take days or weeks — stalling some software projects for as long as nine months, Chiulli and other officials said. That’s a long time to wait for a software upgrade, especially under a process that officials say lack consistent cybersecurity practices, transparency for contractors and visibility for Army leaders into what’s actually happening on their networks. “We have had to do a lot of weird janky things to get code into our environments,” Chiulli said. Sometimes, he said, “I’m not sure how they’re getting code over to us.” The root of the problem, officials said, is that the Army has lacked a single, standardized, centralized process for bringing commercial software onto its secure networks. Instead, “it was up to every program manager,” explained David Markowitz, the service’s chief data and analytics officer. But many program offices lacked the capability or willingness to conduct cybersecurity assessments of new and unfamiliar code. Rather than evaluate the software themselves, they would wait for another organization to vet the company and officially grant its software Authority To Operate (ATO) on military networks. “A lot of times, organizations in the Army won’t talk to [companies] until they have this ‘golden ATO,’” Chiulli said. That created a kind of Catch-22 : The companies best positioned to win Army software contracts where often the ones that already had them. Meanwhile new, innovative entrants — the kind of companies that the Pentagon’s been courting for over a decade — struggled to navigate the combined complexities of cybersecurity rules, procurement regulations and Army bureaucracy. If a program manager did decide to give a new piece of software a chance, moreover, they rarely had a dedicated, isolated sand box in which t o test it. Instead, they had to bring it onto an Army network and assess it there. That, in turn, required the company’s personnel to get cleared for Common Access Cards (CAC) so they could access the Army system. “We spent a lot of time and energy trying to get people CAC cards simply to help work with us,” Chiulli said. “This is to get rid of all that [and] lower barriers to entry.” Gatekeeper will let companies test their software before they have an Army contract, a program manager sponsoring them or even a formal request for proposals to respond to, the officials emphasized, allowing prospective vendors to identify and address cybersecurity problems before trying to do business with the service. Companies will still need CAC cards to access the platform initially, officials acknowledged. But the Army is finalizing an agreement with the General Services Administration (GSA) to use its Login.gov platform, which allows secure access to government systems for members of the public. “We’re looking at mid-November to have that integrated, at which point we’ll be able to make this actually commercially accessible,” said David Wright, chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center (ASIC). Once a company gets access to the Gatekeeper platfor m, it can upload its software and run it through the Army’s standardized cybersecurity tools, including an AI assessment, offi cials explained. In minutes, the automated system will either tell the company its software passed the test or give detailed, actionable feedback explaining why it failed. Gatekeeper will also include the Army’s DevSecOps software development kit, Wright said, giving companies a secure environment in which to address problems using tools the Army itself has vetted. “The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements,” Wright emphasized, “but more to make the process more accessible and available, so that they can get immediate feedback and understand what it is that needs to be adjusted or corrected before these things are brought into an Army environment.”

Compare that with the current, cumbersome clearance process that can take days or weeks — stalling some software projects for as long as nine months, Chiulli and other officials said. That’s a long time to wait for a software upgrade, especially under a process that officials say lack consistent cybersecurity practices, transparency for contractors and visibility for Army leaders into what’s actually happening on their networks.
“We have had to do a lot of weird janky things to get code into our environments,” Chiulli said. Sometimes, he said, “I’m not sure how they’re getting code over to us.”

The root of the problem, officials said, is that the Army has lacked a single, standardized, centralized process for bringing commercial software onto its secure networks. Instead, “it was up to every program manager,” explained David Markowitz, the service’s chief data and analytics officer.

But many program offices lacked the capability or willingness to conduct cybersecurity assessments of new and unfamiliar code. Rather than evaluate the software themselves, they would wait for another organization to vet the company and officially grant its software Authority To Operate (ATO) on military networks.
“A lot of times, organizations in the Army won’t talk to [companies] until they have this ‘golden ATO,’” Chiulli said.

That created a kind of Catch-22 : The companies best positioned to win Army software contracts where often the ones that already had them. Meanwhile new, innovative entrants — the kind of companies that the Pentagon’s been courting for over a decade — struggled to navigate the combined complexities of cybersecurity rules, procurement regulations and Army bureaucracy.

If a program manager did decide to give a new piece of software a chance, moreover, they rarely had a dedicated, isolated sand box in which t o test it. Instead, they had to bring it onto an Army network and assess it there. That, in turn, required the company’s personnel to get cleared for Common Access Cards (CAC) so they could access the Army system.
“We spent a lot of time and energy trying to get people CAC cards simply to help work with us,” Chiulli said. “This is to get rid of all that [and] lower barriers to entry.”

Gatekeeper will let companies test their software before they have an Army contract, a program manager sponsoring them or even a formal request for proposals to respond to, the officials emphasized, allowing prospective vendors to identify and address cybersecurity problems before trying to do business with the service.

Companies will still need CAC cards to access the platform initially, officials acknowledged. But the Army is finalizing an agreement with the General Services Administration (GSA) to use its Login.gov platform, which allows secure access to government systems for members of the public.

“We’re looking at mid-November to have that integrated, at which point we’ll be able to make this actually commercially accessible,” said David Wright, chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center (ASIC).

Once a company gets access to the Gatekeeper platfor m, it can upload its software and run it through the Army’s standardized cybersecurity tools, including an AI assessment, offi cials explained. In minutes, the automated system will either tell the company its software passed the test or give detailed, actionable feedback explaining why it failed.
Gatekeeper will also include the Army’s DevSecOps software development kit, Wright said, giving companies a secure environment in which to address problems using tools the Army itself has vetted.

“The idea here is not to lessen the security requirements,” Wright emphasized, “but more to make the process more accessible and available, so that they can get immediate feedback and understand what it is that needs to be adjusted or corrected before these things are brought into an Army environment.”

Chiulli described the current process as a patchwork of procedures that can leave companies struggling to get software evaluated without already having access to military networks. The Army has resorted to "weird janky things" to move software into its systems, he said. At times, officials could not readily determine how code had been transferred. Under previous arrangements, companies often had to establish access to government infrastructure and learn Army security practices before they could demonstrate a product. Officials said some program offices were reluctant to consider vendors that did not already have an Authority to Operate, effectively favoring companies with existing government relationships. The initiative follows a broader Army effort to cut acquisition red tape and bring commercial technology to soldiers faster , which military leaders outlined earlier this year. Gatekeeper is intended to replace those arrangements with a standardized testing process that lets developers identify vulnerabilities and correct them before moving software toward use on Army networks. At launch, Gatekeeper will still require a Common Access Card, or CAC, the military credential that outside developers have often needed to work on government systems. Chiulli said the Army has sometimes issued those cards to entire teams of civilian developers simply to allow them to transfer software. "Sometimes companies have a hundred developers in the back end that are not necessarily going to have CAC cards," Chiulli said. "And sometimes we give all those people CAC cards simply so that they can do it and commit to us." David Wright, a chief engineer at the Army Software and Innovation Center, said the service expects to integrate the General Services Administration's Login.gov system by mid-November. That would make Gatekeeper accessible to commercial developers without military credentials. Officials estimated that 40 to 50 companies are already encountering obstacles Gatekeeper is designed to address. The Army has also worked with defense startups through its xTech program , supporting projects involving AI-enabled sensors, predictive maintenance and other emerging technologies. The platform will provide an isolated environment, separated from operational Army networks, where developers can upload software for conventional cybersecurity screening and an AI-assisted review. Officials said companies could receive feedback within minutes, correct identified problems and resubmit their code. The system uses established Army software security pipelines, including tools already used by other military services. Passing the scans would not, by itself, grant final authorization to operate on military networks. During the roundtable, Military.com asked how much money and manpower the Army expects to save by reducing the need to issue CACs to civilian developers. "I don't know what that number is," Chiulli said, declining to offer an arbitrary estimate. Wright said the workload is spread among numerous program offices, making it difficult to calculate the time spent arranging credentials for outside contractors. "I know that subjectively it feels like the answer is a lot," Wright said. David M. Markowitz, the Army's deputy chief information officer and chief data and analytics officer, said some major software programs can take six to eight months before developers have an initial working capability. He added that larger programs can cost millions of dollars per month. Those expenses reflect broader software development efforts, not the specific cost of issuing CACs. Officials did not provide an estimate of Gatekeeper's potential savings. The Army is also working through how it will protect companies' proprietary code, particularly when they submit software before securing government contracts. Wright described nondisclosure agreements and controls to keep different vendors' code separate, but said some arrangements remain unresolved. Officials maintained that faster access would not reduce cybersecurity standards. The effort comes amid broader Pentagon investments in cybersecurity and moves toward more consistent security requirements for defense contractors under the fiscal 2026 defense legislation. Whether Gatekeeper delivers the promised efficiencies will become clearer after the wider commercial rollout, which the Army is targeting for November. extraction.body: Chief technology officers gathered for a panel at TIME’s Executives of the Year Impact Dinner: Tech & Data on Tuesday night in New York City and discussed the ways that technology has shifted how their companies operate. Speaking on the panel at the TIME forum were Franziska Bell, CTO and executive vice president of The Home Depot; Fiona Tan, CTO of online marketplace giant Wayfair; and Sam Dozor, CTO of global e-commerce company Rokt, which sponsored Tuesday’s event. Bell emphasized “always being grounded in the consumer experience” when thinking about how to adapt to new and emerging technologies, or what she described as “the art of the possible.” One new AI tool that The Home Depot has deployed is Magic Apron, an “AI empowered home improvement expert,” Bell explained, that can help customers locate items in store, answer how-to questions about products, and respond to images uploaded by users. Applications like Magic Apron, which Bell says has been rolled out in 2,000 U.S. stores, result from Bell assessing the “friction” involved in customer experiences and working to reduce it with technological tools. She did not, however, discount the crucial roles that humans play alongside tech. “I’m a huge believer in human-AI teams,” Bell said. “That’s really where the magic happens.” Tan also spoke about the customer experience at Wayfair and how technology has been leveraged to help consumers figure out what they want from the company’s wide selection of products. “A lot of times people don’t know what they’re looking for, they can’t describe it, and so perhaps we offer you a journey that will resonate,” she said. “We have to also innovate and provide them an experience that speaks more to them.” When it comes to hiring new employees who can tackle consumer experience goals and integrate AI into their work, Tan stressed the importance of “adaptability” in young candidates who can seamlessly adjust to the quickly changing tech landscape. Tan also said that it’s important to pair younger generations with older ones who have more experience at their companies. Dozor said that the moment is prime for companies to invest in technology. “The time is here,” he said. “The time is now, and all of us need to live it.” One of the ways Rokt does this is by expanding the variety of work its employees can do using AI. “It’s amazing to see engineers lean into building product specs and designers writing code,” he said. In that spirit, Rokt, he explained, takes a forward-looking approach to its work, always thinking about what’s next for its employees and what they can accomplish. “Times are changing quickly,” Dozor said, and people can choose to live in the past, present, or future. “We’ve chosen to live six months from now.” TIME Impact Dinner: Executives of the Year: Tech & Data was presented by Rokt.

extraction.body: Chief technology officers gathered for a panel at TIME’s Executives of the Year Impact Dinner: Tech & Data on Tuesday night in New York City and discussed the ways that technology has shifted how their companies operate. Speaking on the panel at the TIME forum were Franziska Bell, CTO and executive vice president of The Home Depot; Fiona Tan, CTO of online marketplace giant Wayfair; and Sam Dozor, CTO of global e-commerce company Rokt, which sponsored Tuesday’s event. Bell emphasized “always being grounded in the consumer experience” when thinking about how to adapt to new and emerging technologies, or what she described as “the art of the possible.” One new AI tool that The Home Depot has deployed is Magic Apron, an “AI empowered home improvement expert,” Bell explained, that can help customers locate items in store, answer how-to questions about products, and respond to images uploaded by users. Applications like Magic Apron, which Bell says has been rolled out in 2,000 U.S. stores, result from Bell assessing the “friction” involved in customer experiences and working to reduce it with technological tools. She did not, however, discount the crucial roles that humans play alongside tech. “I’m a huge believer in human-AI teams,” Bell said. “That’s really where the magic happens.” Tan also spoke about the customer experience at Wayfair and how technology has been leveraged to help consumers figure out what they want from the company’s wide selection of products. “A lot of times people don’t know what they’re looking for, they can’t describe it, and so perhaps we offer you a journey that will resonate,” she said. “We have to also innovate and provide them an experience that speaks more to them.” When it comes to hiring new employees who can tackle consumer experience goals and integrate AI into their work, Tan stressed the importance of “adaptability” in young candidates who can seamlessly adjust to the quickly changing tech landscape. Tan also said that it’s important to pair younger generations with older ones who have more experience at their companies. Dozor said that the moment is prime for companies to invest in technology. “The time is here,” he said. “The time is now, and all of us need to live it.” One of the ways Rokt does this is by expanding the variety of work its employees can do using AI. “It’s amazing to see engineers lean into building product specs and designers writing code,” he said. In that spirit, Rokt, he explained, takes a forward-looking approach to its work, always thinking about what’s next for its employees and what they can accomplish. “Times are changing quickly,” Dozor said, and people can choose to live in the past, present, or future. “We’ve chosen to live six months from now.” TIME Impact Dinner: Executives of the Year: Tech & Data was presented by Rokt.
